column4: Computerization Program
column6: DepEd Computerization Program is the Department’s strategic initiative to modernize the Philippine basic education system by bridging the digital gaps in public schools and offices. Its core mission is to provide equitable, appropriate, and sustainable Information and Communications Technology (ICT) solutions that enhance teaching, learning, governance, and operations. Moving beyond a traditional supply-driven model, the program now employs an evidence-based, needs-responsive allocation system. This strategic shift ensures that technology resources—ranging from individual devices to shared laboratories—are deployed based on actual school size, personnel requirements, and infrastructure readiness, thereby maximizing public funds and ensuring that ICT assets are utilized effectively where they are needed most. The project also includes providing connectivity for schools to enable full utilization of digital tools and platforms for teaching, learning, and administrative functions.

column6: The Republic Act 11396 requires State Universities and Colleges to prepare and implement a Land Use Development and Infrastructure Plan (LUDIP) that shall include the construction of dormitories for students and housing sites for employees. Dormitories are one of the important extracurricular educational facilities that should be present on the campus. Living on campus greatly affects the students’ academic and interpersonal lives. Based on the experiences of the students, it has been shown that students living on campus tend to earn better grades and have retention rates at their institutions that are higher than their off-campus peers. These students are timelier in their graduation and more often go on to graduate school and earn advanced degrees. Living on campus gives students an academic edge by earning higher grades, providing opportunities for learning communication and faculty access, and promoting their future growth by helping them stay connected to the college environment. Staying in a student dormitory reduces the area's carbon footprint by avoiding the need for students to commute or burn gasoline to get to the campus. This will also save them time from sitting in traffic and trying to check their notes while traveling.

column4: “MUSEYO Musuanensis  – A NATURAL and ANTHROPOLOGICAL MUSEUM OF CMU “(Formerly: Proposed "Museyo Musuanensis - A Natural and Anthropological Museum of CMU" Building with FFE
column6:
The proposed project is the Construction of a Two-storey state- of- the – art Museum situated at Central 
Mindanao University specifically at the entrance of the Mt. Musuan Zoological and Botanical Garden (MMZBG) 
which will be labelled “Museyo Musuanensis – A Natural History and Anthropological Museum of CMU”. The 
museum will highlight the different mountain ecosystems of Mindanao by featuring the Mindanao’s unique 
flora and fauna which play significant role in the daily lives of the indigenous peoples or local people living in 
the vicinity of these mountain ecosystems. This natural history museum shall create general awareness on 
the conservation and sustainable use of the natural heritage in Mindanao. 
 
       This museum shall contain at the first floor:  
a. Receiving area with a display depicting the story-line of the Museum;   
b. Mini-theater for gatherings (lectures, seminars, etc.) and a place for orientation regarding the 
storyline of the Museum, rules & statement of policies which will be disseminated museum to the 
visitors; 
c. Biological displays (Botanical and Zoological) depicting biodiversity 
d. Office space for the Museum Head, and the different curators which will be divided into cubicles but 
is adjacent to a conference area for holding meetings; 
e. Office space for the Museum staff; 
f. Processing room for biological and anthropological items; 
g. Reading room and cataloguing & database room;  
h. Storage room for curated Zoological and Anthropological collections; 
i. A souvenir shop with a cozy canteen featuring slow organic food. 
 
     The second floor of the building will contain: 
a. Botanical, Zoological and Anthropological displays; 
b. Anthropological and cultural displays (7 tribes of Bukidnon); 
c. CMU President’s Memorabilia and CMU’s accomplishments; 
d. CMU Herbarium (CMUH) with the numerous herbarium cabinets which is officially indexed in Index 
herbariorum;
e. View deck featuring the surrounding landscape. 
 
The Museum will contain interactive displays which should be friendly and understandable to elementary pupils 
and the general public. There should be one flow for the museum visitors starting with an entrance and an exit 
which should clearly be designated. 
 
The Museum should be able to accommodate a maximum of 50 visitors at a given time and museum tour can 
last for 1 hour.   
 
Executive Summary:  
 
At present, Central Mindanao University has a University Museum which sits on the oldest and delapidated 
building of said institution. However, this University Museum serves as the repository center for the 
conservation of the biological and anthropogical materials of Mindanao. The rich biological and anthropological 
items are housed in the University Museum and were obtained through collaborative efforts of the researchers 
of CMU from various fields and implemented through collaborations of various stakeholders. This University 
Museum has 3 sections viz., Botany, Zoology & Anthropology (based from CMU Code Chapter 5. Article 8. 
Section 3.) which hold respective collections. Currently, there are about more than 10,900 specimens in the 
Botany Section; 8,300 specimens in the Zoology Section and about 600 artifacts in the Anthropology Section. 
These collections are expected to rise as on-going researches are being implemented which are not only 
funded by CMU but by other funding institutions like CHED and DOST-PCAARRD. Simultaneously, 
collaborations with indigenous groups and local people are pursued viz., Manobo- Matigsalog Tribal Council 
of Elders Cityof Davao, Inc. (MAMATRIPCEDI). 
 
More importantly, the herbarium of the Botany Section holds an official acronym CMUH which is listed in the 
Index Herbariorum, a listing of the recognized herbaria all over the world.  
 
With the considerable number of holdings / collections found in our Museum, there is therefore an urgent need 
to house these in a more spacious and appropriate building. If these collections can be presented in a well
organized manner, the collections can really convey to the public the rich flora and fauna which our Mindanao 
mountain ecosystems possess of which the rich culture of the indigenous peoples and local people who 
depend so much on these natural resources can be showcased to the public. This will develop appreciation 
among the general public and inculcate the need to conserve and sustainably use these resources.  
 
The word “Musuanensis” is taken from Musuan, the sitio on which Central Mindanao University is situated and 
this university has the famous and obvious landmark which is Mt. Musuan. The suffix –ensis is added which 
adapts the rule in taxonomic nomenclature which adds such suffix if the name is taken from a place or certain 
geographical location. Taxonomic nomenclature is latinized regardless of their derivation hence the name of 
the museum is “Museyo Musuanensis”. This name also reflects the major activity of the Museum which is 
taxonomic in nature.

column4: Construction of Information Management and Security System Center
column6:
The proposed investment is a critical measure to transform Pampanga State Agricultural University (PSAU) into a globally competitive institution by modernizing our Information Technology (IT) ecosystem. This initiative, moving beyond simple system upgrades, is a strategic commitment to digital infrastructure designed to ensure that PSAU students and faculty can effectively cope with the accelerating pace of international technological and academic advancements. The goal is to facilitate the most effective, efficient, and secure delivery of services to all PSAU clientele and stakeholders, aligning the university’s operational and educational capabilities with global professional standards.

This comprehensive project is anchored by critical components necessary for sustained growth and international academic alignment. The core of the transformation is the establishment of a centralized IT data management facility and the laying of a fiber optic backbone and robust network infrastructure. This foundational digital structure is essential to support the high-speed information management system required for real-time academic resource access, massive data processing for advanced research, and seamless administrative functions. This action directly supports the global agenda of SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure) by building resilient digital infrastructure and aligns with the Philippine Development Plan's (PDP) goal of digital transformation, ensuring our graduates are digitally proficient and internationally competitive.

To guarantee uninterrupted educational and research continuity, the project also includes the installation of new power transformers and electric distribution lines, ensuring a dependable, stabilized supply of energy across the campus. Furthermore, enhancing public safety is paramount for an optimal learning environment: the installation of strategically located, high-definition CCTV security systems will create a safer and more secure campus. This security component directly supports SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions) by promoting safe learning environments and strengthening efficient institutional management, which are fundamental prerequisites for achieving high-quality education.

By executing this strategic IT upgrade, PSAU achieves a crucial objective: providing its diverse student body—particularly those from socio-economically disadvantaged backgrounds—with the necessary digital tools and high-speed connectivity to engage on a global level. This investment ensures equitable access to worldwide academic resources, facilitates international collaboration in research, and ultimately equips graduates with the digital literacy and technical agility required to compete successfully in the modern, globalized workforce. This modernization effort is therefore not just an operational necessity but a commitment to social equity, ensuring every PSAU student has the platform to succeed internationally.

column4: Construction of a Two-Storey Instruction and Research Laboratory Building for Civil Engineering
column6:
The proposed two-storey Civil Engineering Laboratory Building is designed to support advanced instruction, research, and community training in alignment with modern engineering standards. The facility will house five specialized laboratories: (1) Advanced Geotechnical Engineering Laboratory, (2) Structural Engineering Laboratory, (3) Hydraulics and Water Resources Engineering Laboratory, (4) Advanced Material Testing Laboratory, and (5) Engineering Simulation and Computing Laboratory. These laboratories are complemented by a dedicated ICT-enabled training room, faculty rooms, a student lounge, a laboratory technician’s room, and a viewing/observation deck for safe monitoring of laboratory activities.
The facility will feature highly specialized infrastructure essential for civil engineering experimentation, including a strong floor–reaction wall system for structural load testing, overhead crane installation for lifting heavy specimens and equipment, vibration-controlled testing zones, reinforced foundations for large-capacity machines, and safety-compliant storage for laboratory materials. Across its two floors, the building will provide three gender-inclusive comfort rooms, and designated parking and open circulation areas. The facility is designed for at least 400 (200M/200F) students, 15 faculty (7M/8F), and 5 technical personnel at peak use.
Universal design principles will be applied, including PWD ramps, tactile guides, accessible restrooms, and senior-friendly seating. Gender and Development (GAD) principles will be integrated through inclusive spaces, proper lighting, safety features, and dedicated wellness corners.
Equipment to be procured includes advanced geotechnical, structural, hydraulic, and materials testing systems; high-performance computers; simulation software; digital displays; ICT equipment; laboratory furniture; and safety fixtures.
Climate-responsive design features, such as natural ventilation, solar shading, rainwater collection, and energy-efficient lighting, will ensure resilience and sustainability. The building aims to serve as a modern regional hub for hands-on learning, research, and innovation in civil engineering.

column4: Construction of Digital Learning Spaces Center for World Class Education
column6:
Overview/Description: 
The project obtained 40 Million GAA funding in 2024 for Phase I and 100 Million as per NEP in 2026 for Phase II. The proposed 2027 budget will implement the Phase III of the project.
The project is a climate-smart three-storey building, with each storey having 4,000 square meter floor size for a total floor size of 12,000 square meters. This facility will house the Student Curricular and Non-Curricular Activity Spaces, Digitized Training Halls and Classrooms in support of the internationalization of the Visayas State University , integrating consciousness of gender issues in the Gender Resource Center, and the Quality Assurance Center.
The Student Curricular and Non-Curricular Activity Spaces will include Student Councils space, Multi faith Room, Mental Health Hub, Smart Classrooms, Conference rooms, student recreational lounge, international student lounge, Training room, digital mini-auditorium, atrium and activity center, and a showcase (exhibit) area.
The Gender Resource Center will include the Anti-Sexual Harassment Office with offices for staff, conference room, and Private or confidentiality reception room, and counseling rooms.
The Office of the Director for Quality Assurance with offices for staff, Conference room, evaluation room, and records room.
The building will have elevator and ramp for PWD access and comfort rooms for all gender including PWD, a large parking area and mini park. The building will provide internet access and other ICT equipment for the student and other stakeholders. 
Digitalization of the facility will involve the integrated systems to automate service delivery and facilities and resources management.
The building will be a green building that will have a rain harvesting facility that will make the building sustainable in terms of water resources. The design of the building will consider weather patterns and natural lighting. Solar panels will be integrated in the design of the building for energy sustainability.
The site for building construction will be near the National Highway that will be easily accessible by all stakeholders
Purpose:
This multi-purpose is a facility for various curricular and non-curricular activities that could not be accommodated in any buildings in the main campus.  The concept of an integrated academic and non-academic environment where students learn the values of social interaction and and guided governance of the affairs of students. The center will serve mainly as indoor learning spaces for different student indoor activities where students are supported with resources, particularly when ASEAN Integration programs are implemented. Local students can join national or international activities especially covering academic and non-curricular expositions, conferences and conventions. All 7000 plus students of the University where 65% are females and 35% males will have equal access to the facilities and amenities of the building.
Gender Resource Office will serve as one stop center for all things related to gender in response to various national mandates and houses the offices for the Gender Programs.  Serves as clearinghouse for all VSU programs/projects/activities on gender-responsive curriculum development/research and extension.
Quality Assurance Center which will serve as a hub for the university's numerous activities aimed to assure the quality of its programs in instruction, research and extension. column4: Construction of School of Medicine Building
column6:
The proposal of Tarlac State University to institute a School of Medicine and offer Doctor of Medicine program aims to expand and create new curricular program to support the different regional, national, and international academic goals that promote a better sustainable future for all. 

Among the Sustainable Developmental Goals included in the 2030 agenda for sustainable development, Sustainable Developmental Goals 3 (SDG 3) aims to ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for individuals at all ages and focuses on human health. All goals are interrelated and implementing the 2030 agenda that requires a multi-stakeholder, multi-sectoral, and multi-actor response that would require the engagement and commitment of all sectors, as opposed to the traditional top-down, single-sector approach. (Ancharya, 2020) 

Similarly, the Ambisyon Natin 2040 has laid down four areas for the realization of strategic policies, and projects over the next 25 years which are building a prosperous, predominantly middle-class society where no one is poor, promoting a long and healthy life, becoming smarter and more innovative, and building high-trust society.  

In response to the Sustainable Developmental Goals 3 (SDG 3) and Ambisyon Natin 2040, the Province of Tarlac has bolstered its provision of premium health care and services especially to those who struggle financially and those at the fringes of the society who are severely affected by the pandemic, and other diseases. 

Despite these efforts, there are still insurmountable challenges that the province is facing such as the shortage of healthcare professionals especially in the various municipalities, and with-it insufficient healthcare services. However, because of the provincial government good governance, basic health care is provided to municipalities and barangays with high incidence of various health issues and conditions. Hence, it remains a priority for both the local government units and the university in ensuring the health and well-being of Tarlaqueños by providing training, information campaign, education, and extension services. This is done in the hope that in this process, the LGUs and the university contributes to eradicating poverty and promote economic growth in the province.  


The Republic Act No. 11223 is an Act that instituted the universal Health Care for All Filipinos, which prescribe the necessary and immediate reforms that are aimed to improve the health care system in the country.  

One of the objectives of the said law is to facilitate the training of more health care professionals, including doctors, nurses, and other health care workers, to address the burgeoning scarcity and migration of health care professionals in the country. The collaboration between the Department of Health (DOH) and the Local Government Units to provide more affordable, equally effective, and efficient health care system is central in crafting approaches that will mitigate the medical needs of the Filipinos.  

Vital to this endeavor is the partnership forged between the Department of Health, Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), Philippine Regulation Commission (PRC) and the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) in facilitating the upskilling needs of health care professionals who will address the needs of all the citizens across the country. The Commission on Higher Education is mandated to regulate and assure the quality of education and training given to medical professionals in-training in various higher education institution and health science schools across the country. The Tarlac State University has been serving the country for 119 years since its establishment in 1906, and for 36 years as chartered university. Among its program that contributes to the number of health care professionals in the province, region, country and internationally are the well-trained nurses of the Bachelor of Science in Nursing, and other pe-med courses such as BS Chemistry. With this, the university now aims to expand its academic services into educating and training of well-trained Doctor of Medicine for the province, for the region and for the country.

The institution of Doctor of Medicine program in Tarlac State University is grounded on the health conditions and situations faced by the residents of the Province of Tarlac. The School of Medicine of the university will lead the formation, training and graduation of well-trained and competent doctors who will augment the burgeoning needs of doctors in the province and in the region. Through the TSU School of Medicine, the 17 municipalities and Tarlac city will be served even while students are on their education and on-going training through the supervision of the faculty members. This will ensure the continued good health education of community residents and support the pragmatic plans to build a better life and better future among residents of Tarlac province and other adjoining areas.  	 


Based on the consultation and discussion of the Committee on the Medical Program of the University, with its intent to offer the Doctor of Medicine Program in the university, a consortium with the University of the Philippines College of Medicine shall be formed. The main objective of the consortium is to aid the development of the new program’s curriculum, training and hiring of staff, and basis for the acquisition of the required resources as stipulated in the CHED Memorandum Order No. 18, s. 2016 (Policies, Standards, and Guidelines for the Doctor of Medicine (M.D) Program). This consortium shall be formed and implemented while the School of Medicine building, a vital component for the full offering of the program, is still under construction.

The infrastructure of the School of Medicine is included in the initial infrastructure proposals of TSU as identified on page 110 of the institution’s Land Use Development and Infrastructure Plan (LUDIP) 2020~2030. Initially, the proposed building shall be constructed on a 1653.30 m2 lot area at the Lucinda Campus and is adjacent to the College of Science Building. However, since the University is planning for a land expansion in the Lucinda Campus, the School of Medicine building shall be relocated to the 2.5-hectare land to be acquired. The members of the LUDIP technical working group are currently training for the LUDIP enhancement; hence, the relocation plan and the detailed floor plan for the School of Medicine building shall be finalized once the acquisition of land and land title transfer is completed, and in turn be integrated into the LUDIP enhancement in 2025 by the LUDIP technical working group.  

The proposed School of Medicine Building is a six (6)-storey structure and has a total floor area of 4,668 m2; each floor has an area of 778 m2 and has space for utility/electrical room and gender-neutral and PWD-friendly restrooms.

The ground floor of the building shall be allocated as an area for the lobby, information counter, elevator, and stairs. The majority or approximately 1323.30 m2 of the ground floor shall be allocated as parking space for faculty, staff, personnel, and students. In line with the required resources and facilities stipulated in the CMO No. 18, s. 2016 and based on the benchmarking activities held with state universities offering the said program, the following offices, rooms, and laboratories shall be constructed in the various floors of the proposed building: dean’s office, admission office, cashier office, accounting office, faculty office, supply office/photocopy area, medical library, computer laboratory, student organization office, cafeteria, lecture rooms, skills laboratory, simulation facilities/laboratories (Operation Room, Delivery Room, Patient Ward), clinical laboratory with biosafety cabinet, chemistry laboratory, microbiology laboratory, molecular laboratory, research laboratory facility, donning and doffing areas, dissection room, and cadaver storage room. At the top floor of the building is the roof deck which shall be used as a recreational area.

The estimated CO expenditure in constructing the building is PHP 303,000,000.00; construction shall commence in 2029 and is estimated to be completed in 2030. The estimated MOOE expenditure for 2026 is estimated to be PHP 61,000,000.00 which comprises disbursements in procuring fixtures, furniture, lecture and laboratory equipment, human resource expenditures, and operating costs. In particular, the CMO No. 18, s.2016, and the recommendations from the benchmarking activity present the following medical equipment to be procured for the School of Medicine building: biosafety cabinet, dissection tables, cadaver tables, simulation mannequins, hospital bed, cadaver table, microscopes, histology slides, demonstration slides, timer, basic glassware, hot plate, blender/osterizer, spirometer, urinometer, hemocytometer with accessories, instruments for animal experiments, and electrocardiograph. In addition, audio-visual equipment for lecture rooms shall also be procured.  

The estimated operating and sustainability cost of offering the medical program is PHP20,000,000.00. As a whole, it is projected that PHP384,000,000.00 is required to construct, procure, and sustain the infrastructure, equipment, and human resources needed in offering the Medicine program of TSU.  

The expected output of this proposal is the six-storey Medicine Building, the procurement of equipment and the acquisition of human resources essential to the implementation of the Medical Program of TSU.

column4: Construction of Culture and Arts Center (Digos Campus)
column6:
This establishment will be the center of the college for the acquisition, conservation,
research, communication, and exhibition of the tangible and intangible heritage of the
Indigenous Peoples in Davao del Sur. Davao del Sur is the habitation of the three major
Indigenous People (IP) communities: the Bagobo-Tagabawa, Blaan, and Kalagan (Provincial
NCIP). These indigenous communities though distinct from each other in language, are the
same in their richness of cultural heritage. However, because of the current trends of
globalization and lifestyle, even of education, this richness has been devalued by the younger
generation. As observed, there are many indigenous youths who do not speak their
indigenous language for several reasons. When language is lost, their tradition will also
disappear soon after. Then, eventually, if not salvaged, there will be an extinction of culture.
This is a two-story fully airconditioned building which has comfort rooms and other amenities
that will cater all genders, PWDs and senior citizens. There will be six rooms in this building;
four (4) rooms are for display of artifacts, arts and crafts, and other indigenous material
collections, one (1) receiving room, and one (1) viewing room. The viewing room will serve as
the audio-visual room for presentations of recorded data relevant to the indigenous culture of
Davao del Sur and its environment. The receiving room will be spaciously designed that can
accommodate limited visitors with appropriate distancing when still in the pandemic. The
three (3) rooms for display will be labeled according to the names of the three (3) major IP
groups present in the province which are the Bagobo-Tagabawa, Blaan, and Kalagan. The other one will be the display room of all other
indigenous materials that can be found in the province coming from different IP communities
other than the three major groups mentioned above.
This Cultural Heritage Center, shall cater students, stake-players, local community
members, and local and foreign tourists. This center will become one of the icons of
tourism in the province of Davao del Sur.

column4: Establishment of 8-Storey Smart  Academic Building with Specialized Laboratories,(Phase 1, Phase 2 and Phase 3), (USTP  CDO)
column5: University of Science and Technology of Southern Philippines
column6:
The proposed 8-Storey Smart Academic Building is a forward-thinking infrastructure designed to address the educational needs of 21st-century learners. Recognizing the technological aptitude of today’s students, the building will integrate advanced instructional materials and cutting-edge facilities to foster a dynamic and innovative learning environment. This initiative aligns with the University of Science and Technology of Southern Philippines (USTP) mission to deliver quality education rooted in advanced science and technology, addressing stakeholders' expectations for excellence in higher education.

The building will feature specialized state-of-the-art laboratories and equipment, including a DAT-SCI-TECH Research Laboratory, Data Analytics Program Laboratory, Computational and Data Center, upgraded Energy Testing and Analysis Laboratory, Soil and Water Laboratory Equipment, enhanced High Energy and Plasma Physics Laboratory, and Advanced Materials and Testing Laboratory. Additionally, it will include innovative agricultural technologies such as Crop Care Equipment, Drone, Drip & Sprinkler Systems, and a Soil and Product Analytical Laboratory.

This infrastructure directly responds to the growing demand for modernized classroom and laboratory spaces at the USTP Cagayan de Oro Campus, where the lack of physical facilities continues to challenge the delivery of quality education. Despite the gradual transition from online to face-to-face learning, many students remain disadvantaged due to limited internet access and the absence of personal devices. The establishment of this building emphasizes the importance of returning to in-person instruction, which fosters a more interactive and immersive learning experience, significantly benefiting those who struggle with remote learning.

Aligned with the USTP Framework 2030, the Philippine Development Plan, and the Regional Development Investment Program (RDIP), this project aims to address Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) such as Quality Education (SDG 4), Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure (SDG 9), and Reduced Inequalities (SDG 10). The building's design incorporates climate-resilient infrastructure, ensuring sustainability and functionality in disaster-prone environments.

By providing advanced facilities and fostering a collaborative environment, the Smart Academic Building will enhance the university's capacity to deliver internationalized education, support gender and development (GAD) initiatives, and cater to the global and local demands for higher education and advanced research. This project embodies USTP’s vision for a transformative learning environment that not only meets the region's educational needs but also elevates the institution’s level of quality education, as outlined in its 2030 Vision and Eight-Point Agenda.

Ultimately, this initiative underscores USTP's commitment to bridging the gap in physical infrastructure while empowering students, faculty, and stakeholders through innovative and inclusive education. It is a pivotal step in addressing classroom shortages and transitioning to face-to-face learning for a more equitable, engaging, and impactful academic experience.

column4: Construction of Fifteen (15) Storey Engineering Tower, BatStateU Alangilan
column6:
The proposed project involves the construction of a fifteen (15) storey Engineering Tower at Batangas State University (BatStateU) – Alangilan Campus. The 26,095.00 sq meter facility is designed to meet the growing demands of the university’s engineering programs by providing modern classrooms, specialized laboratories, faculty offices, and collaborative learning spaces. The tower will enhance educational quality, foster research and innovation, and support partnerships with local and national industries, positioning BatStateU as a leading institution for engineering education in the region.
BatStateU Alangilan currently faces limitations in accommodating its expanding engineering programs. Existing classrooms and laboratories are insufficient for the growing student population and lack modern equipment for advanced research. These constraints hinder high-quality teaching, practical training, and large-scale research initiatives. The proposed tower will address these needs by providing a purpose-built facility equipped for modern engineering education.
The tower will be built within the Alangilan Campus in Batangas City, Philippines, a strategic and accessible site that allows for the building footprint, supporting facilities, and future expansion while minimizing disruption to ongoing campus activities.
Target Population / Beneficiaries:
• Engineering Students: Approximately 5,000 students will benefit from enhanced classrooms, laboratories, and study spaces.
• Faculty and Researchers: Access to modern facilities for teaching, experimentation, and collaboration.
• University Community & Industry Partners: Strengthened research outputs, workforce readiness, and collaborative opportunities for technological innovation.
This is a public higher education infrastructure project and a medium- to high-rise institutional building, designed in accordance with national building codes, structural standards, safety regulations, and environmental guidelines.

An additional component of the proposed facility is designed to serve as a practicum and training laboratory for students enrolled in the Bachelor of Science in Nursing. Over time, the birthing facility is envisioned to operate as an income-generating unit, enhancing the University’s financial sustainability.

column4: CONSTRUCTION OF THREE-STOREY SCHOOL BUILDING, COLLEGE OF EDUCATION, PHASE 2 AT MAIN CAMPUS
column6:
Under Republic Act No. 10229, Catanduanes State University (CatSU), through its College of Education, is authorized to operate its Laboratory Schools in accordance with the joint regulatory oversight of the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) and the Department of Education (DepEd). CHED Memorandum Order No. 35, s. 2016, allows State Universities and Colleges (SUCs) with approved laboratory schools to accommodate up to 750 students and to offer Grades 11 and 12 as part of their instructional mandate.

As a recognized Teacher Education Institution (TEI), CatSU offers five undergraduate teacher education programs. In line with CHED Memorandum Order No. 52, s. 2007, all TEIs must operate a cooperating school, which in CatSU’s case is its Laboratory Schools. These serve as essential venues for practicum and field studies, providing pre-service teachers with hands-on teaching experience vital to their professional development.

The original infrastructure initiative, titled "Construction of Two-Storey Main Campus Senior High School Building, College of Education Laboratory Schools, Phase I", received funding under the General Appropriations Act (GAA) 2024, specifically implemented by the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) through a special provision for SUC-related infrastructure. Phase I of construction commenced in early 2025, with an anticipated completion timeline set before the end of the same year.

However, following a CHED memorandum dated December 18, 2023, state universities and colleges (SUCs), except those operating laboratory schools, were directed to discontinue offering senior high school programs starting School Year 2024-2025, as the legal basis for SUC's involvement in basic education had ended with the K-12 transition period from SY 2016-2017 to SY 2020-2021. The discontinuance of senior high school in SUCs was because there was no longer legal basis to fund the same. This policy change rendered GAA funding for general SHS programs in SUCs no longer valid.

This policy shift prompted a change in the building’s intended use: originally planned for Senior High School cohorts, the facility is now reallocated to maximize utility within the College of Education laboratory schools—including classrooms, teaching, and administrative support.

Industries today operate in highly dynamic environments, with state-of-the art technologies, equipment and workspaces. A three-storey building will house specialized laboratories, classrooms, income generating projects of the college and workshop equipment with industry standard tools and equipment. column4: Completion of BukSU Hotel Training Laboratory for BSHM
column6:
Presently, only Phase 1 of the BukSU Hotel Training Laboratory has been completed. The existing structure has a total gross floor area of 225 square meters, of which 170 square meters serve as usable floor area, the primary working space for students and instructors. Despite its limited size, the facility has provided a more realistic and industry-aligned learning environment for students, allowing them to simulate actual hospitality operations and develop essential technical skills. On this account, the BSHM program continues to experience steady student enrollment, signaling increasing confidence in the quality of BukSU’s hospitality education. At present, the program has enrolled a total of 614 students across all year levels, consisting of 227 males and 387 females, for the first semester of AY 2025–2026. Given the available area, the training laboratory can accommodate a maximum of 25-30 students per class. While this setup ensures adequate workspace and safety within the available area, the current 225-square-meter structure and limited facilities cannot keep pace with the growing number of students and the program’s expanding instructional requirements.
Furthermore, the facility’s timeworn equipment and restricted floor area hinder the full integration of hands-on learning experiences aligned with industry standards.

Consequently, many students have limited opportunities to work with up-to-date hospitality technologies and tools, reducing their exposure to real-world operations and innovation practices that are critical for industry readiness. More importantly, the completion of the existing structure has become an urgent need due to the deterioration of the structural integrity of the first floor caused by the unfinished second floor. The cause of the deterioration is that the seepage of rainwater from the unroofed upper level has begun to affect the integrity of the first storey, leading to moisture infiltration and potential corrosion of steel reinforcements. In addition, prolonged exposure to these conditions may weaken the concrete components and may cause further degradation of interior materials, such as ceilings and wall finishes. Without immediate intervention, these structural issues could escalate, compromising not only the facility’s safety and functionality but also the university’s prior investments in the project.

To address this issue, the completion of the BukSU Laboratory building is necessary to provide a more conducive learning environment, enhance practical training opportunities, and ensure that male and female students receive quality education aligned with industry requirements. Thus, the completion of the BukSU Hotel Training Laboratory is both an academic and structural imperative. Finishing the remaining phases will ensure that the facility can fully support BukSU’s growing BSHM program, meet industry-aligned training standards, and preserve the long-term integrity of the existing building.

For the completion of this project, a total amount of Php 62,500,000.00 is needed, which will cover the construction of additional floors, installation of modern equipment, interior finishing, and procurement of furnishings. This funding will also include provisions for safety systems, accessibility features, and energy-efficient utilities to ensure that the facility meets current building and educational standards. Once completed, the fully operational Hotel Training Laboratory will serve as a comprehensive venue for hands-on instruction, skills assessment, and industry collaboration, ultimately strengthening BukSU’s capacity to produce highly competent graduates who can meet the evolving demands of the hospitality and tourism sectors.

Improvements will include enhanced connectivity provisions, reconfigured learning spaces for collaborative and project-based learning, and compliance with accessibility standards under BP 344. These interventions will enable the building to serve as a modernized learning hub that supports both traditional and technology-driven instruction.

This project directly contributes to the Philippine Development Plan’s sector outcomes of expanding access to quality education, strengthening human capital, and improving infrastructure resilience. By ensuring that technology education facilities are safe, functional, and future-ready, the University can better equip learners with the competencies needed to thrive in a globally connected, innovation-driven economy. column4: CONSTRUCTION OF RUMINANT RESEARCH AND INSTRUCTIONAL FACILITY AT PANGANIBAN CAMPUS
column6:
The College of Agriculture and Fisheries (CAF) at Catanduanes State University offers a Bachelor of Science in Agriculture majoring in Animal Husbandry, a program that requires adequate instructional facilities to bridge theoretical learning with field-based application. Currently, the lack of a dedicated ruminant facility limits the College’s ability to maintain and properly house large animals such as cows, carabaos, and bulls, which are essential for laboratory exercises, livestock management training, and applied research. This deficiency not only affects the quality of instruction but also poses risks to animal welfare, especially during typhoons and other severe weather conditions common in Catanduanes.

The proposed construction of a Ruminant Research and Instructional Facility at Panganiban Campus will directly address this gap by providing a purpose-built shed and support infrastructure designed for the proper housing, care, and management of large ruminants. The facility will be equipped with designated areas for feeding, watering, and veterinary care, alongside provisions for manure management to ensure environmental compliance. Beyond serving as a shelter, it will function as a living laboratory where students can conduct hands-on activities in breeding, nutrition, and animal health management under controlled and safe conditions.

To complement instructional needs, the facility will also support applied research and extension activities related to dairy and meat production. By integrating a small-scale dairy production component, students and faculty will gain practical exposure to milk handling, processing, and quality assurance practices, while also generating outputs that can be used for demonstration, training, and potential community-based livelihood projects. These activities will foster innovation in sustainable livestock production, particularly in resource-constrained island environments.

At a broader scale, the establishment of this facility will strengthen the university’s capacity to produce graduates who are well-prepared to address the challenges of animal husbandry in rural and agricultural economies. By institutionalizing structured training, research, and technology transfer in livestock production, the project supports inclusive agricultural growth, enhanced food security, and improved resilience of farming systems—outcomes that are consistent with national development priorities on human capital development, rural productivity, and sustainable agricultural modernization.

column4: RETROFITTING AND EXPANSION OF COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES ACADEMIC BUILDING AT MAIN CAMPUS
column6:
The existing College of Health Sciences (CHS) building at Catanduanes State University currently accommodates twenty-two (22) classrooms that are utilized for academic purposes, aside from administrative purposes. Several of these rooms serve critical functions such as the Dean’s Office, Faculty and Accreditation Room, Research and Extension Room, Laboratories, Amphi Room, Medtech Laboratories, CHS/JR Room, NDRs, FNLs, while the remaining spaces have been converted into specialized areas including Simulation Rooms, Anatomy and Physiology Room, Audio-Visual Rooms, and TESDA Accreditation facilities. Due to this configuration, there are insufficient dedicated classrooms for core subjects, resulting in the University’s reliance on facilities of the Nutrition and Dietetics building located on the opposite side of the campus. This arrangement has posed logistical challenges, particularly for students and faculty who must traverse significant distances under varying weather conditions, affecting both efficiency and academic productivity.

The increasing enrollment at CHS has further intensified the demand for academic space, creating a shortage that compromises the delivery of specialized health science courses. With plans to open new degree programs such as Bachelor of Science in Midwifery, Bachelor of Science in Medical Technology, and Bachelor of Science in Public Health, the current infrastructure is insufficient to accommodate the projected student population and curricular requirements. Accreditation recommendations from AACCUP have also emphasized the necessity of modern, state-of-the-art facilities, particularly with classrooms that meet the prescribed 7x9 meter dimensions to support 40 students per room, thereby aligning with national standards for higher education delivery.

In addition to classroom space, compliance with accreditation and international standards requires purpose-built laboratories. For instance, a Nursing Skills Laboratory must meet the prescribed size of 8m x 14m (112 square meters) to qualify for Level IV accreditation and ensure alignment with ASEAN integration requirements. The retrofitting and expansion of the existing CHS building address these gaps by providing appropriately sized, well-equipped lecture and laboratory spaces capable of supporting current and future programs. This ensures not only regulatory compliance but also the advancement of the college’s academic and training capacity.

Once completed, the expanded CHS Academic Building will centralize instructional, administrative, and laboratory functions in a single, purpose-designed facility. This integration will reduce inefficiencies associated with dispersed learning environments, improve accessibility for students and faculty, and foster a more conducive setting for instruction, research, and clinical training. By supporting the delivery of high-quality education in the health sciences, the project strengthens institutional capability to produce competent graduates who can respond to the growing demand for healthcare professionals locally, nationally, and regionally, thereby addressing broader human capital development objectives.

column4: ESTABLISHMENT OF NURSERY AND ORCHARD FOR IMPROVING PRODUCTIVITY AND BIODIVERSITY AT PANGANIBAN CAMPUS
column6:
Catanduanes, located along the eastern frontier of the Philippines and facing the Pacific Ocean, is characterized by its strategic isolation, high exposure to typhoons, and significant natural endowments. Despite being situated within the typhoon belt, the province retains relatively rich biodiversity and forest resources, making it one of the remaining ecological frontiers of the Bicol Region. The island province of Catanduanes has a land area of 1,492.16 square kilometers (about 149,216 hectares) and had a population of 271,879 as of the 2020 Census of Population and Housing. As of the 2024 Census, the population decreased to 261,169, reflecting a negative growth rate of about, 0.96% annually from 2020 to 2024.

Crop production in Catanduanes, however, remains limited both in diversity and volume. Catanduanes remains known for its production of abaca, coconut, rice, peanut, and lowland vegetables among its major crops. While these crops remain vital to the local economy and subsistence, fruit and vegetable production is insufficient to meet the daily nutritional needs of the population. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), a healthy diet includes at least 400 grams of fruits and vegetables per person per day to reduce risk of noncommunicable diseases. Recent studies show that in the Philippines, fruit and vegetable intake is substantially below this recommended level across all socio demographic groups.

At present, the Provincial Environment and Natural Resources Office (PENRO) serves as the sole institutional provider of planting materials across the province. However, the supply remains inadequate in both volume and diversity, with no established private sector engagement in large-scale plant breeding, propagation, or nursery enterprises. Only a small number of fruit-bearing tree seedlings are commercially available, often at prohibitive costs, thereby constraining the expansion of local orchards and reducing agricultural productivity. This scarcity of accessible planting materials contributes to underutilization of arable lands and limits opportunities for diversifying farm incomes.

In response to these constraints, Catanduanes State University (CatSU) proposes the establishment of a nursery and orchard within its Panganiban Campus. The nursery will serve as a center for producing high-value vegetable seedlings, fruit-bearing trees, and hardwood species, including threatened or endangered varieties critical for biodiversity conservation. The orchard will function as a complementary facility, supplying scion materials for propagation and supporting research-based cultivation practices. Beyond its role in seedling and orchard development, the project will serve as an instructional laboratory and demonstration area for the Bachelor of Science in Agriculture program, consistent with Commission on Higher Education (CHED) requirements. By integrating research, instruction, and extension, the project will address the shortage of planting materials, contribute to improved food security, and enhance biodiversity conservation, while fostering broader community resilience and sustainable rural development.

Provisions include a mini-grocery and reasonably priced dining facilities operated by the campus’s Community Business Operations (CBO) unit, thereby creating a self-contained and student-friendly environment. Rental arrangements will follow an all-inclusive package covering basic utilities such as water, electricity, and gas, with optional connectivity services for phone and internet. This structure provides financial predictability for students and families, minimizes hidden costs, and allows students to focus more effectively on their academic responsibilities.

Beyond fulfilling immediate accommodation needs, the dormitory is envisioned to strengthen the institutional sustainability of CatSU by serving as an income-generating project under the CBO framework. The project also reflects the university’s compliance with Executive Order No. 75, s. 2019, by utilizing its assets in ways that directly contribute to institutional resilience and service delivery. Under General Requirements, the project covers Mobilization and Demobilization activities, securing all necessary Permits and Clearances, and implementing Construction Safety and Health measures throughout the duration of the work. It also includes the provision of Temporary Facilities to support operations, as well as the preparation and submission of complete As-Built Drawings upon project completion.

For Site Work, the scope involves the Removal of existing Structures and Obstructions within the project area, followed by Excavation activities amounting to 89 cubic meters. This is complemented by Embankment works totaling 108 cubic meters, and the placement of 115 cubic meters of Gravel Fill to ensure proper grading and site preparation.

For Plain and Reinforced Concrete Work, the scope includes the placement of 47 cubic meters of Structural Concrete (Class A, 28 days), along with the installation of 5,248.63 kilograms of reinforcing steel bars to ensure structural integrity. The work also covers the provision and installation of all necessary formworks and falseworks required for proper shaping and support during concrete casting.

The Finishing and Other Civil Works include the application of Soil Poisoning for termite protection, along with 186.00 square meters of Masonry Works and 372.00 square meters of Cement Plaster Finish to complete the wall surfaces. The scope also covers 1,556.89 square meters of Painting Works, 323.71 square meters of Tiling Works, and 2,970.00 square meters of Floorcreting Works. Additionally, the project involves the installation of Plumbing Works and Fixtures, the setting up of a Fire Sprinkler System, and the inclusion of Landscaping improvements. The fabrication and installation of Built-Up Letters and Logo are also part of the overall finishing requirements.
For Metal Works, the scope includes the fabrication and installation of 176.28 linear meters of metal railings and ladder components, providing both safety and accessibility within the project site. It also covers 795.64 square meters of cladding works to enhance exterior and interior surfaces, along with 5,886.27 kilograms of steelworks required for structural and architectural elements.

Under Electrical Works, the project involves the installation of various lighting fixtures to ensure adequate illumination throughout the facility. It also includes the provision and setup of the Fire Detection and Alarm System (FDAS) to ensure compliance with safety standards and enhance fire protection within the building.

For Doors, Windows, and Glassboards, the scope includes the supply and installation of all required doors and windows to complete the building’s enclosure and access points. It also covers the installation of glassboards to support instructional, operational, or administrative functions within the facility.

Under Furniture, Fixtures, and Equipment, the project involves the installation of Airconditioning Works to ensure proper cooling and ventilation, as well as Electronics and Communication Works to support the building’s operational systems. Additionally, the scope includes the supply and installation of an elevator to enhance accessibility and vertical mobility within the structure.

column4: The Schools of Living Traditions/Institutes of Living Traditions/Intangible Cultural Heritage Program
column5: National Commission for Culture and the Arts
column6:
The National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) will continue to implement the School of Living Traditions (SLTs) alongside other related initiatives to support the ongoing efforts in safeguarding Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) in the Philippines. These activities will be expanded in the coming years, fostering stronger partnerships with community-based organizations, people's organizations, local government units, and cultural communities.

Key activities, including capacity-building, assessments, training workshops, updating of ICH inventories, and monitoring of inscribed cultural elements, will be sustained. Special focus will also be placed on the documentation of ICH present within the SLTs and their respective communities to further protect and promote these valuable traditions.

The NCCA will provide continuous support for the implementation of the SLTs over the next five years (Years 0 to 5), along with the development and production of learning guides to ensure effective transmission of cultural knowledge from cultural masters to learners. In addition, the NCCA will work to document the unique art forms of each cultural community. As part of its strategic outreach, technical assistance will also be provided to potential partners interested in establishing new SLTs in various regions of the country, thereby extending the reach of this initiative.

Further, in times of emergencies, the NCCA will offer vital assistance to communities focused on ICH by providing support for the repair and maintenance of SLT centers, as well as ensuring that cultural masters receive the necessary resources to continue their artistic creations. As SLTs advance, each will assess and revisit its sustainability strategies to evaluate progress, refine their approach, and gather valuable insights to improve the current SLT framework for long-term success.

The proposed Gender-Responsive Poultry Housing of Kalinga State University requires a well-planned site that supports efficient poultry operations while ensuring safety, accessibility, and inclusivity for all users. To ensure effective chick management, a Brooding House must include:

30–50 sqm brooding area with ergonomic equipment

6–8 sqm feed storage room with accessible shelving

3–4 sqm sanitation and handwashing station

4–6 sqm observation corner for student learning

For growing and finishing operations, the Grower/Finisher House must include:

60–100 sqm growing pens with non-slip flooring and adjustable feeders

6–8 sqm equipment storage with lightweight tools suited for women and men

2 sqm biosecurity footbath station for disease control

The Layer House intended for egg production should provide:

80–120 sqm layer cages or deep-litter area with safe egg-collection height

10–12 sqm egg processing area with ergonomic workstations

6–8 sqm egg storage room for proper handling

4–6 sqm cleaning/sterilization area to maintain hygiene

Support facilities that enhance inclusivity and safety for all genders must also be integrated into the layout, including:

20–30 sqm training/orientation room for mixed-gender learning

10–15 sqm rest or shaded waiting area suitable for women, elderly, and pregnant participants

6–8 sqm gender-neutral toilet accessible to all

Handwashing stations at multiple entry points positioned at comfortable heights

Finally, appropriate waste management systems must be established to comply with environmental standards and support sustainable production. These include:

20–30 sqm manure drying area

10–12 sqm composting or vermicomposting area

A properly designed septic tank

Together, these spaces create a holistic, gender-responsive poultry facility that promotes safety, comfort, learning efficiency, and equitable participation of all KSU students, faculty, and community trainees.

column4: Completion of Seed System Facility, Entienza Campus - Phase 2
column6:
The Entienza Campus of CNSC located in Sta. Elena, Camarines Norte is the campus farthest away from the Main Campus and from the administrative capital of Camarines Norte. This is also one of the youngest delivery units which was established in 2007. At present, it has approximately 500 student population and about 25 faculty and staff. Most of the students in CNSC Entienza Campus are either from Sta. Elena, Camarines Norte or the nearby municipalities of Quezon province such as Calauag, Lopez and Gumaca, Quezon. It offers academic programs on entrepreneurship and teacher education. 
Among the Colleges or delivery units of CNSC, the Entienza Campus is the least developed specifically in terms of adequacy of infrastructure. Due to limited funding from income and from the regular agency fund of CNSC, the construction of additional academic buildings in this campus remained less of a priority for the past years. 
To minimize inequity in terms of the development of the six (6) campuses of CNSC, the prioritization of developmental initiatives was reviewed and is now directed to the development of satellite campuses including Entienza Campus. 
A Seed System Facility (building) in Entienza Campus was first constructed in 2012 (through DA-BAR funding) but was not sustained due to inadequate fund and limited cash resources. Hence, the building remains unutilized. 
At present, this building needs to be completed in preparation for the resumption of face-to-face classes in 2022. The completion of this Seed System Facility is expected to boost the number of classrooms in the campus which at the moment is only six (6). Six (6) classrooms will not be adequate to accommodate the 500 students expected to report in the campus with the potential resumption of face-to-face classes in 2022. Hence, this construction project needs to be completed by 2022 in preparation for the resumption of such mode of classes and also in anticipation of the growing student population of Entienza Campus. 
Moreover, the completion of this infrastructure project will provide Entienza Campus with laboratory facilities that can be used not just for instruction purposes but also for research of faculty members and students.
Being a delivery unit that has been left behind for a long time in terms of infrastructure development, this project is also expected to boost the morale and inspire its faculty, staff and students to continue strive for excellence in everything that the institution does.

column4: CONSTRUCTION OF THREE-STOREY UNIVERSITY REGISTRAR'S BUILDING AT MAIN CAMPUS
column6:
The Catanduanes State University’s Office of Admission and Registration Services (OARS) has been operating within the University’s Main Building since its establishment. While it has functioned adequately in providing admission, enrollment, and academic records management, the current space is no longer sufficient to meet the operational demands of a rapidly expanding student population. As of the first semester of SY 2025–2026, the University serves a total of 15,853 students — 15,147 from the Main Campus and 706 from the Panganiban Campus. The increasing enrollment volume, coupled with the complexity of academic record-keeping, degree audit, transfer evaluation, course scheduling, and compliance with data privacy regulations, necessitates a dedicated facility designed to support both administrative efficiency and student service quality.

The proposed three-storey University Registrar’s Building is envisioned as a purpose-built facility that will house the OARS on the ground floor, equipped with cashiering windows, service counters, and an adequately sized waiting area to facilitate orderly transactions and minimize congestion. The second floor will serve as a secured records storage area, with climate-controlled conditions and fire-resistant materials to ensure the preservation of vital student records, documents, and institutional archives. The third floor will accommodate the Guidance Counselling and Testing Office, including dedicated spaces for psychological testing, career assessments, and student development programs. This integrated layout consolidates related student service units, streamlining processes and improving inter-office coordination.

This project directly contributes to the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023–2028 sector outcome of “Enhanced access to quality education” and “Improved efficiency of education service delivery.” By investing in modernized registrar and guidance facilities, the University strengthens its institutional capacity to manage academic data, facilitate student progression, and uphold service standards aligned with digital transformation initiatives in higher education. Moreover, the project is developmental in nature as it addresses infrastructure gaps, optimizes administrative workflow, and provides an enabling environment for data-driven decision-making, thereby supporting the long-term growth of the institution and enhancing student welfare. The facility will not only improve operational resilience but also position the University to respond effectively to future increases in enrollment and evolving educational demands.

column4: Construction of  Two-Storey Male Dormitory in Fortune Towne Campus
column5: Carlos C. Hilado Memorial State University
column6:
V.	PROJECT DESCRIPTION

The proposed two-storey male dormitory at Carlos Hilado Memorial State University (CHMSU) Fortune Towne Campus will address the need for affordable, safe, and gender-responsive housing. Designed to comply with safety standards, it will foster academic success and personal growth in a secure, inclusive environment.

Aligned with gender and development guidelines, the dormitory will promote discipline, collaboration, and community engagement. Its sustainable design uses eco-friendly materials, enhancing the university’s appeal, student retention, and satisfaction. This initiative supports male students' academic focus, socioeconomic opportunities, and holistic growth while contributing to the institution’s financial stability and reputation.

Phasing with Scope of Work:
Phase 1: Pre-Construction
•	Site clearing and preparation.
•	Mobilization of workforce and materials.
•	Securing necessary permits and compliance with local building regulations.
Phase 2: Construction
•	Structural Works (foundation, framing, and roofing)
•	Architectural Works (walls, partitions, flooring)
•	MEFPS (Mechanical, Electrical, Fire Protection, Plumbing and Sanitary systems)
•	Finishing Works (installation of fixtures, furniture, and dormitory equipment)
•	Phase 3: Post-Construction
•	Final inspections and quality assurance testing
•	Turnover of the facility to the university administration

The proposed two-story male dormitory at CHMSU Fortune Towne Campus is designed to provide a safe, inclusive, and conducive living environment for students. 

Key features include:

1.	Room Options
1.1 International/PWD Room: Designed for international students or those with disabilities, this room accommodate two occupants with single beds and feature private en-suite shower and toilet facilities. The rooms are fully accessible, with PWD-friendly accommodations such as ramps and handrails, ensuring a comfortable and inclusive living space.
1.2	Shared Rooms: These four rooms are equipped with bunk beds and offer shared toilet and bathroom facilities. Designed to foster community living, these rooms provide an affordable yet functional housing option, with separate and well-maintained common restrooms to ensure privacy, hygiene, and inclusivity for all residents.
2.	PWD Accessibility
Equipped with ramps, handrails, and PWD-friendly rooms to ensure accessibility for all residents.
3.	Study Area
Dedicated collaborative and individual learning spaces on each floor to support academic success.
4.	Laundry and Drying Area
A small laundry room with washing and drying facilities will be included, allowing residents to manage their laundry within the dormitory.
5.	Dining Area
A designated space offering meals, snacks, and a venue for social interactions.
6.	Lobby and Reception Area
A welcoming lobby with a dedicated reception desk for resident inquiries and support.
7.	Stock Room
Stock or storage room will be designated for the safekeeping of maintenance equipment and supplies
8.	Security Features
24/7 security services, including CCTV monitoring, fire alarms, and secure access systems, ensuring a safe environment.
9.	Wi-Fi Connectivity
High-speed internet access throughout the dormitory to support academic and personal online activities.
10.	Emergency Features
Clearly marked fire exits and evacuation plans for safety during emergencies.
11.	Sustainability Elements
Designed with eco-friendly materials and energy-efficient systems to minimize environmental impact.
These features are designed to create a balanced environment that prioritizes student comfort, safety, and academic performance.

column4: Construction of Machinery Laboratory and Testing Center
column6:
The Machinery and Testing Laboratory will be basically composed of two 
laboratories, which are: (1) Metals Fabrication Laboratory and (2) Materials Testing and 
Analysis Laboratory. The Metals Fabrication Laboratory will house various equipment for 
metal fabrication processes, such as, machining, milling, planning, bending, grinding, 
welding, and drilling machines. On the other hand, the Materials Testing Laboratory is 
where the analytical equipment for materials analysis will be housed. These equipment 
includes grinding and polishing machines, metallurgical microscopes, universal testing 
machine, cut-off wheel machine, muffle furnace, specimen mounting machine, and 
hardness testers. This laboratory will also be used by students for their laboratory 
exercises.
 Because of the large dimension of the various equipment in the Metals Fabrication 
Laboratory, the laboratory will have a warehouse-type design with a high ceiling in which 
an overhead crane will be placed for moving these heavy equipment. On the other hand, 
the Materials Testing and Analysis Laboratory is basically a standard-type laboratory room 
with chairs and tables where the students can do their laboratory exercises using the 
various laboratory equipment which will be placed at the corners of the room. To 
maximize the space of the proposed building, a multi-purpose area which can be used as 
an observation deck for Metals Fabrication Laboratory will be constructed exactly above 
the Materials Testing and Analysis Laboratory. This area will also be used for various 
purposes such as training, seminars, presentations, etc.
 As a backgrounder, the College of Engineering has been selected for the 
establishment of the Metals and Engineering Innovation Center (MEIC) for Region 12. The 
MEIC is basically a Research and Development (R&D) facility which focuses on metals 
fabrication and engineering. The start of the project is expected to commence this year 
(2022). The grant includes the provision of various metal fabrication equipment and 
various equipment for materials testing and analysis. Moreover, the grant will also include 
training of College of Engineering (COE) personnel regarding the use, maintenance and 
repair of various equipment that will be provided. Eventually, the trained personnel from 
the COE will become the future trainers for the identified stakeholders of the center. 
With the various equipment included in the grant for the establishment of MEIC, 
the counterpart of the university is a building that will house all the equipment for 
research activities and training purposes. Thus, the proposed construction of the 
Machinery and Testing Laboratory Building is very timely. However, in the case that the 
MEIC grant will start ahead of the construction of the proposed Machinery and Testing 
Laboratory Building, all the equipment will be temporarily housed and operated in one of 
the Engineering Technology buildings or in one of the Engineering laboratory buildings 
whichever will be found by MIRDC as the most appropriate.

column4: Construction of a Four-Storey EVSU Main College of Arts and Sciences Extension
column6:
Under the Eastern Visayas State University (EVSU) Land Use Development and Infrastructure Plan (LUDIP), the Construction of the Four-Storey EVSU Main College of Arts and Sciences (CAS) Extension Building has been identified as a priority initiative for FY 2025. The project received an initial allocation of P12.5 million under the FY 2025 General Appropriations Act (GAA) and an additional P8 million in the FY 2025 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

The proposed academic building is conceived as a modern, climate-resilient, and inclusive facility designed to expand the instructional capacity of the EVSU Main Campus. It will serve as a temporary transition building to accommodate CAS classes while the existing CAS Academic Building undergoes demolition and reconstruction. Once fully completed, the structure will operate as a central hub for teaching, learning, research, and multidisciplinary collaboration.

Strategically located near the CAAD Building, the four-storey facility integrates seamlessly with the existing campus layout while embedding principles of sustainability, safety, and disaster resilience. The layout consists of:

•	Ground Floor: four (4) lecture rooms, faculty lounge, a students space and a library
•	Second & Third Floors: six (6) lecture rooms on each floor, with dedicated student lounge areas
•	Fourth Floor: four (4) laboratories, two (2) dispensing rooms, one (1) instrument room, and essential support spaces including comfort rooms and utility rooms.

The project responds directly to the significant increase in student enrollment and the need for improved instructional spaces. It integrates inclusive, safe, resilient, and sustainability-driven design strategies aligned with UN SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), and SDG 13 (Climate Action).

As indicated in the EVSU LUDIP Hazard and Risk Assessment, the project site is not susceptible to flooding, storm surge, tsunami, or liquefaction, yet it is categorized as having high susceptibility to landslide and moderate seismic exposure (PEIS VII). The design therefore incorporates robust Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) and Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) interventions to ensure long-term structural integrity and operational continuity.

The Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Change Adaptation Features will include:
1.	Hazard-Responsive Design
o	Structural system designed to withstand seismic events in compliance with the National Building Code and DPWH guidelines.
o	Typhoon- and wind-resilient roofing and façade systems considering Leyte’s high exposure to strong tropical cyclones.
o	Flood-safe floor elevations and reinforced foundations to mitigate pluvial and fluvial flooding risks.
2.	Climate-Adaptive Infrastructure
o	Rainwater harvesting and detention systems to manage peak rainfall events, reduce campus flooding, and support water reuse for sanitation and irrigation.
o	Energy-efficient building envelope (low-E glass, shading devices, natural ventilation corridors) to reduce indoor heat stress and cooling costs.
o	Solar-ready rooftop design to accommodate renewable energy integration for partial power supply and continuity during outages.
3.	Sustainable and Green Campus Integration
o	Permeable paving and bioswales in parking and open areas to reduce surface runoff and recharge groundwater.
o	Green landscaping and tree buffers for shading, carbon sequestration, and windbreaks.
o	Indoor air quality improved through low-VOC materials, cross-ventilation, and natural daylighting.
4.	Safety, Accessibility, and Inclusivity
o	PWD-accessible ramps, elevators, and toilets ensuring compliance with BP 344.
o	Safe, well-lit, and clearly marked emergency exits and evacuation routes.
o	Gender-responsive facilities to promote inclusive use of learning spaces.
5.	Operational Continuity and DRRM Integration
o	Equipped with fire detection, suppression systems, and emergency power backup to ensure academic continuity during disruptions.
o	Integration into the university’s Campus Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan (CDRRMP) with building-specific Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs).
o	Provision of multi-functional spaces that can serve as temporary shelters or emergency command centers in times of disaster.

The proposed building will have a total floor area of approximately 4,466.40 square-meters., designed with adequate air circulation, parking, and PWD-compliant features. The Approved Budget for the Contract (ABC) is P180,488,000.00, inclusive of DRR/CCA-integrated design, sustainable construction materials, and energy-efficient systems to ensure long-term resilience, operational efficiency, and institutional sustainability.

The project duration is 300 Calendar days, subject to government procurement process and availability of funds. Once completed, the four-storey EVSU College of Arts and Sciences Extension is expected to benefit an estimated 760 students per class cycle and approximately 1,520-2280 students per day. This capacity directly supports the campus's increasing enrollment and ensures adequate instructional, laboratory, and learning spaces for all programs.

column4: Construction of Five-Storey EVSU Dulag Academic Building
column6:
The proposed project is one of the priority listed projects for FY2025 under the LUDIP of the university. The Five-Storey Academic Building for Eastern Visayas State University–Dulag Campus (EVSU DC) is a strategic infrastructure investment designed to address the campus’s increasing academic demands, spatial constraints, and long-term sustainability objectives. As student enrollment continues to rise, the existing facilities have become insufficient to support instructional delivery, research activities, innovation programs, and student services. Overcrowded classrooms, limited laboratory spaces, and inadequate academic support areas hinder the campus’s ability to deliver quality, future-ready education.

Given the limited availability of developable land within the campus, the project adopts a vertical expansion strategy to maximize land use efficiency without the need for additional land acquisition. The proposed five-storey building will house modern academic and support facilities, including:

• Flexible classrooms designed for various learning modalities
• Computer and digital laboratories
• Innovation and incubation hubs
• Faculty rooms and academic support offices
• Multi-purpose and collaboration halls
• Student learning spaces and ancillary service areas

These spaces are intended to strengthen the delivery of 21st-century education, support multidisciplinary collaboration, and enhance student and faculty productivity.

As indicated in the EVSU LUDIP Hazard and Risk Assessment, the project site is not susceptible to storm surge and landslide, has a high susceptibility to tsunami and liquefaction, and moderate seismic exposure (PEIS VII) for ground shaking hazard. The design therefore incorporates robust Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) and Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) interventions to ensure long-term structural integrity and operational continuity.

As EVSU DC is situated in a region highly exposed to typhoons, earthquakes, and extreme rainfall events, the building is designed with robust DRR/CCA measures to ensure safety, functionality, and long-term resilience. These include:

1. Hazard-Resilient Structural Engineering
• Structural design compliant with the National Structural Code of the Philippines (NSCP) for seismic and wind loads.
• Typhoon-resistant roofing and façade systems engineered for high-wind exposure common in Eastern Visayas.
• Reinforced structural frame and foundation systems designed to reduce risks from ground shaking and climate-related stresses.
2. Climate-Adaptive Site and Building Features
• Flood-adaptive site planning and elevated floor levels to reduce pluvial and fluvial flood risks.
• Integrated stormwater management systems, including drains, detention tanks, and rainwater harvesting facilities.
• Energy-efficient building envelope with natural ventilation corridors, shading devices, and low-emissivity materials to reduce indoor heat gain.
3. Sustainable, Low-Carbon, and Resource-Efficient Systems
• Solar-ready roofing for future renewable energy integration to ensure partial energy autonomy and lower operational costs.
• Use of green and durable building materials to reduce environmental impact and enhance lifecycle performance.
• LED lighting, efficient HVAC systems, and water-conserving fixtures to promote resource efficiency.
• Green landscaping that serves as heat buffers, carbon sinks, and natural stormwater absorbers.
