The proposed repair/rehabilitation/retrofitting of a two-storey Multi-Disciplinary Learning Center at Catanduanes State University-Panganiban Campus is a crucial initiative aimed at addressing the growing demand for quality education and enhancing the university's capacity to deliver diverse and innovative academic programs. The facility will house modern classrooms, specialized laboratories, faculty offices, research spaces, and digital learning hubs, all designed to support advanced teaching, learning, and administrative functions.

The immediate repair/rehabilitation/retrofitting of the Multi-Disciplinary Learning Center is necessary due to the significant increase in student enrollment and the expansion of university programs, which have placed considerable strain on the existing infrastructure. Overcrowded classrooms and the lack of specialized learning spaces have hindered the effective delivery of technical, science-related, and interdisciplinary courses, impacting student engagement, hands-on learning experiences, and overall academic performance.

A well-designed Multi-Disciplinary Learning Center will play a key role in improving education quality by creating an optimal, technology-integrated learning environment. The facility will feature state-of-the-art laboratories for hands-on science and technology education, smart classrooms equipped with digital learning resources, and collaborative research spaces that will foster innovation and knowledge exchange. Additionally, the center’s design will incorporate sustainable building practices, such as eco-friendly construction materials, energy-efficient lighting, and climate-resilient infrastructure, ensuring its long-term viability and environmental sustainability.

This project aligns with key national and international education frameworks, including the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023-2028, which highlights the role of educational infrastructure in regional growth and competitiveness. It also supports the government's “Build, Build, Build” program, which prioritizes the development of educational facilities in underserved areas to promote equitable access to quality learning. Furthermore, the project adheres to global standards such as the World Bank Education Strategy 2020-2030 and UNESCO’s Education 2030 Agenda, both of which emphasize the importance of investing in inclusive, accessible, and resilient educational infrastructure.

Beyond academic instruction, the Multi-Disciplinary Learning Center will serve as a hub for industry collaboration and community engagement. It will facilitate partnerships with local industries, research institutions, and government agencies, providing students with internship programs, research initiatives, and skill development workshops that bridge the gap between academic learning and real-world applications. These initiatives will enhance students’ employability and entrepreneurial potential, contributing to workforce readiness and regional economic growth.

Moreover, the new facility will help Catanduanes State University-Panganiban Campus meet accreditation standards set by the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), allowing the university to expand its program offerings and uphold national and international academic quality benchmarks. For students in rural Catanduanes, the center will provide enhanced access to higher education, reducing the need to migrate to urban centers for specialized academic and research opportunities.

With its cutting-edge facilities, inclusive design, and industry-driven approach, the immediate repair/rehabilitation/retrofitting of the Multi-Disciplinary Learning Center is essential for accommodating enrollment growth, improving program delivery, and elevating the university’s overall academic standing. column4: CONSTRUCTION OF TWO-STOREY SUPPLY AND PROPERTY MANAGEMENT BUILDING
column6:
Over the past three years (2022–2025), the Supply and Property Management Unit (SPMU) of Catanduanes State University has undergone significant staff expansion alongside a rapid increase in the volume and value of supplies and property under its management. The unit now handles millions worth of deliveries and procurement transactions annually. However, its current office setup and storage areas are no longer sufficient to meet operational needs, especially when serving large-scale purchase orders. The limited space has made inventory handling, receiving, and safekeeping increasingly challenging.

Currently, the SPMU operates in three small rooms located under the University Gymnasium. These makeshift spaces are not only undersized for growing inventory volumes but also pose health and safety risks. One of the rooms serves as a temporary holding area for returned unserviceable properties, which, if not disposed of regularly, can lead to overstocking, clutter, and even the intrusion of animals such as snakes and rodents. Although the unit conducts regular disposal activities at least twice a year, this remains a short-term solution to a long-term space and facility problem.

Two of the existing rooms currently function as storage areas for hardware, janitorial, and electrical supplies and materials. However, due to the increasing volume of deliveries, the Supply and Property Management Unit (SPMU) often finds itself needing to secure additional temporary spaces to accommodate incoming supplies that can no longer fit in the designated stockrooms. These facilities have already exceeded their optimal storage capacity, resulting in overcrowding and logistical difficulties in managing, locating, and distributing supplies efficiently. This situation reinforces the urgent need for expanded and properly designed warehouse space to support the growing operational demands of the unit.

The current SPMU location is also vulnerable to natural hazards. Being situated in a low-lying area, it is prone to flooding, as evidenced by recent typhoons that caused ankle-deep water to enter the office. Additionally, the area is exposed to other adverse weather conditions such as extreme heat and prolonged heavy rainfall due to shearline activity—factors that compromise both employee productivity and the safety and integrity of stored materials. The lack of climate-resilient infrastructure puts both physical inventory and staff at risk, potentially leading to service interruptions and financial losses.

To address these pressing concerns, the proposed construction of a two-storey Supply and Property Management Building will provide a centralized, safe, and functionally designed facility tailored to the operational needs of the unit. The building will include designated stockrooms for various types of supplies—hardware, electrical, janitorial, office, and IT—making inventory management more organized and efficient. The facility will also feature dedicated working spaces for staff, loading and unloading bays, and enhanced security and ventilation systems.

This new facility will not only improve the efficiency and accuracy of supply chain operations at CatSU but also ensure resilience against climate risks, enable better asset protection, and contribute to a more professional, productive working environment. Ultimately, it will support the university’s broader institutional goals in infrastructure modernization, good governance, and service delivery.

column4: CONSTRUCTION OF THREE-STOREY COLLEGE OF MEDICINE AND HEALTH SCIENCES BUILDING AT MAIN CAMPUS

The establishment of the College of Medicine and Health Sciences at Catanduanes State University (CatSU) responds to the urgent need for accessible and high-quality medical education in the province. As the sole state university in Catanduanes, CatSU plays a critical role in producing future health professionals who will address the shortage of physicians and allied health workers across the island and neighboring provinces. The CatSU Doctor of Medicine program is envisioned as a four-year post-baccalaureate course that integrates basic sciences, clinical sciences, and community-based training. By adopting modern and flexible curriculum models—ranging from discipline-based to outcome-based approaches—the program ensures adaptability to emerging trends in medical education while remaining responsive to the local health landscape. Early exposure of medical students to patient care, community health delivery systems, and interdisciplinary practice will be prioritized, strengthening their competencies in both curative and preventive medicine. The proposed facility is therefore designed not only for academic instruction but also to simulate real-world healthcare environments for training future physicians.

Beyond medical instruction, the program emphasizes research, innovation, and leadership in healthcare delivery. The building will support inter-professional and multi-professional learning approaches, equipping students with the skills required to work collaboratively in diverse health systems. Facilities will also accommodate research initiatives focused on pressing local health issues, thereby producing evidence-based strategies that can improve health outcomes for underserved populations. By integrating leadership, management, and population health in the curriculum, the College will ensure that its graduates are not only clinically competent but also capable of shaping healthcare policies and practices in the region.

The construction of this facility directly supports broader socioeconomic goals by expanding the province’s capacity to produce homegrown medical professionals who are more likely to serve in their local communities. Improved access to health education and training will reduce the long-term dependency on external human resources and contribute to stronger healthcare resilience, particularly in geographically isolated and disaster-prone areas like Catanduanes. column4: ESTABLISHMENT OF CATSU DAGAY CHILDMINDING CENTER AT MAIN CAMPUS
column6:
The challenge of balancing parenthood with academic or professional responsibilities is a recurring issue in both higher education institutions and workplaces. Instances where students attend classes with toddlers or employees bring children into the office highlight the absence of adequate childminding facilities, which directly affects productivity and learning outcomes. Without institutional support, parents—particularly mothers—are forced to divide their attention between caregiving and responsibilities, often resulting in reduced efficiency and missed opportunities for academic or professional advancement.

National policies reinforce the urgency of addressing this concern. Executive Order 340, s. 1997 mandates government agencies and government-owned and controlled corporations to provide day care services for children under five years of age, while Republic Act 9710 or the Magna Carta of Women (MCW) obligates institutions to develop mechanisms that reduce the dual burden of work and family care. Despite these mandates, implementation remains uneven across government institutions, underscoring the need for Catanduanes State University (CatSU) to establish a dedicated childminding center as part of its compliance with national directives and commitment to gender-responsive governance.

Evidence from international and local studies demonstrates that the absence of childcare support disproportionately impacts women. The IFS Deaton Review on Inequalities (2021) indicates that women’s employment and work hours drop significantly after childbirth, while men’s remain largely unchanged. In the university context, this translates into lower retention rates for female students and reduced performance for employees managing both caregiving and professional obligations. By providing a structured facility that supports parents, the proposed CatSU Dagay Childminding Center directly enhances workforce participation, academic persistence, and institutional productivity—factors that contribute to human capital development and more inclusive economic growth.

Functionally, the establishment of a childminding center will create a safe, nurturing, and developmentally appropriate environment for children of students, faculty, and staff. The facility will not only mitigate stress and improve focus among parents but also foster inclusivity by ensuring that family responsibilities do not become barriers to education or employment. In doing so, CatSU strengthens its role as a transformative institution—one that not only delivers academic services but also enables broader socio-economic outcomes aligned with long-term national development goals.

column4: RENOVATION/RETROFITTING AND CONSTRUCTION OF THREE-STOREY EXTENSION OF GENERAL ADMINISTRATION BUILDING AT MAIN CAMPUS
column6:
The General Administration Building of Catanduanes State University (CatSU), constructed in the early 1970s, was built prior to the adoption of modern seismic and structural codes. As such, the building lacks critical provisions for earthquake resistance now required by the National Structural Code of the Philippines (NSCP). Currently serving as the university’s central administrative hub, the building houses core operational units, including the Central Management Division, Administrative and Financial Affairs Division, several Academic Affairs offices, and those under Research, Extension, and Production Affairs. Its structural reliability is vital to maintaining uninterrupted governance and support services critical to the university’s academic and operational functions.

Recent structural evaluations and engineering inspections have revealed significant deterioration in key load-bearing components, notably in the reinforced concrete beams and slabs at the upper levels. These deficiencies, primarily due to prolonged exposure and reinforcement corrosion, pose serious safety risks, particularly in the event of seismic activity. Given Catanduanes’ location within a seismically active zone, the absence of retrofitting interventions constitutes a major hazard to both human life and institutional continuity. Although previous allocations was secured for the building's improvement, the funding proved insufficient to cover the full technical requirements of a seismic retrofit and the necessary structural improvements. The university is therefore seeking additional funding for comprehensive retrofitting and the construction of a three-storey annex to address both structural deficiencies and space constraints.

The proposed project adopts an integrated approach that addresses risk reduction, climate resilience, and accessibility. The retrofitting design will comply with the latest NSCP and DPWH guidelines, while the extension will be equipped with energy-efficient and climate-adaptive features, such as on-grid solar photovoltaic systems, rainwater harvesting infrastructure, and modern fire detection and alarm systems. Universal design principles will also be applied, including the installation of an elevator and barrier-free access for persons with disabilities and senior citizens. These enhancements are consistent with the government’s commitment to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), disaster resilience, and inclusive infrastructure development.

column4: Construction of Academic Building for College of Technologies - IT Department
column6:
The Information Technology (IT) Building is a pivotal infrastructure project that underscores Bukidnon State University’s strategic commitment to advancing digital competency, innovation, and academic excellence in information and communications technology (ICT). In response to the growing global demand for ICT professionals—driven by rapid developments in digital transformation, software engineering, cybersecurity, and data science—the university recognizes the urgent need for a modern, purpose-built facility. This initiative aims to provide a state-of-the-art academic and training space that will support advanced technical instruction, research, and innovation in the ICT field. Strategically located within the university’s College of Technologies, the IT Building will serve as a central hub for cultivating digital talent. With a total footprint of 995 square meters, a gross floor area of 4,975 square meters, and five floors capable of accommodating up to 735 students, faculty, and support staff, the building is designed to meet the growing educational and technological needs of BukSU. Its capacity ensures a dynamic learning environment where students can engage in hands-on training, collaborative projects, and immersive technology-based learning experiences.

For Phase 1 of its construction, an amount of Php 100,000,000.00 is required to initiate the development of the ground floor of the Information Technology Department Building. This initial phase will focus on establishing the core structural and functional components that will form the foundation for subsequent phases of the building. The construction will include essential facilities such as computer laboratories, networking
and server rooms, and collaborative learning spaces, ensuring that students have early access to modern IT infrastructure and hands-on learning environments even as the building continues to be completed. The building will host advanced computer laboratories for programming, networking, and system administration; smart classrooms supporting hybrid and technology-enhanced learning; and innovation hubs and collaborative workspaces that foster interdisciplinary teamwork, startup incubation, and student-led technology projects. 
Additionally, the IT Building will feature server and network infrastructure for cloud computing, cybersecurity exercises, and enterprise simulations, alongside faculty offices that support academic leadership, research, and mentorship. These facilities are designed to integrate seamlessly with industry-aligned technologies, enabling students to develop competencies in software development, data analytics, artificial intelligence, and information security. Beyond equipping students with technical expertise, the IT Building is aligned with BukSU’s vision of becoming a SMART University. By providing modern infrastructure, the project empowers learners, faculty, and researchers to lead digital transformation initiatives, foster innovation ecosystems, and contribute to regional ICT development in Northern Mindanao and beyond. Ultimately, this facility will not only enhance the university’s educational capacity but also strengthen its role as a key driver of technological advancement and workforce readiness in the digital economy.
For the first phase of construction, a budget allocation is required to complete the ground floor of the IT Building. This phase focuses on establishing essential functional spaces that will immediately support administrative operations and academic coordination. The ground floor will include a dedicated faculty room to provide instructors with a collaborative and comfortable working environment, a storage and archive area to ensure the safe keeping of academic records and resources, and a dean’s office to facilitate effective academic leadership and management. Completing these
components will allow the university to begin partial operations in the building while subsequent phases are underway. By prioritizing these foundational spaces, the first phase ensures that key administrative and academic functions are fully supported from the outset. The completed ground floor will serve as the operational backbone of the IT Building, enabling faculty, staff, and administration to carry out their responsibilities efficiently.
This phased approach not only accelerates the building’s functional readiness but also aligns with BukSU’s broader goal of establishing a modern, technology-driven learning environment that will benefit both students and educators from the very beginning of the project.

column4: Planetarium Upgrade to Level-up Science Awareness and Relevance (Project PULSAR)
column5: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration
column6:
The Department of Science and Technology - Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (DOST-PAGASA), through its Space Science and Astronomy Section (SSAS), has been a pivotal force in fostering public engagement with astronomy. A cornerstone of  this outreach is the provision of Planetarium Shows, offered at a nominal fee of 25 pesos per person. This accessible pricing structure enables the agency to cater to a diverse audience, encompassing individuals of all ages, socioeconomic backgrounds, and cultural affiliations.

However, the sustained operation of these valuable programs faces challenges due to the inevitable wear and tear of aging Planetarium equipment. Specially, concerns have been raised regarding the current quality of shows, with the digital projector being slow and faulty, audio equipment malfunctions, and laptop failures, which significantly compromise the audience experience. The targets of this project are to improve the quality of the Planetarium Shows and enhance the Planetarium experience of its audience, create more educational opportunities at low cost for students and the general public, and increase engagement with Astronomy.

Project PULSAR (Planetarium Upgrade to Level-up Science Awareness and Relevance) is a strategic initiative to transform the DOST-PAGASA Planetarium in Quezon City into a leading center for science engagement and education. A quantitative, comparative analysis will be conducted employing a pre-and post-intervention design utilizing audience surveys. The survey will focus on identifying the audience satisfaction level and the perceived educational value of the Planetarium show before and after. An independent sample t-test will be used for inferential statistical analysis to determine statistically significant differences in measured variables.

column4: Hydrological and Hydrogeological Assessment of Water Resources in SOCSARGEN: Strategic Foresight for Sustainable Domestic and Irrigation Water Supply
column6:
Water security is an emerging challenge in the SOCSARGEN region—comprising South 
Cotabato, Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, Sarangani, and General Santos City—where rapid urban 
development, expanding agricultural activities, and the adverse effects of climate change are 
placing growing stress on freshwater resources. These pressures are particularly concerning for 
communities that rely heavily on water for domestic use, irrigation, and economic productivity, 
especially in agriculture-dominated provinces. 
At present, the region faces significant knowledge gaps in both surface and subsurface 
water dynamics. While some areas have access to river systems and shallow wells, others 
depend on deep aquifers whose recharge capacities and long-term sustainability remain 
uncertain. The lack of comprehensive hydrological and hydrogeological data hinders the ability 
of local government units (LGUs), water districts, and planners to make informed decisions. 
Without accurate assessments, risks such as groundwater depletion, contamination, over
extraction, and inefficient water distribution may go unaddressed—leading to water shortages, 
reduced agricultural yields, and increasing conflict over access.
 This project aims to provide a science-based foundation for sustainable water 
governance in the SOCSARGEN region by conducting a thorough hydrological and 
hydrogeological assessment of its water resources. It will identify and map key aquifers, 
watersheds, and recharge zones; analyze water quality and seasonal availability; and evaluate 
the vulnerability of both surface and groundwater systems to climate variability and land-use 
changes.
 Through this initiative, MSU-General Santos aims to build a strong scientific foundation 
for sustainable and inclusive water governance in the region. By identifying high-risk zones, 
projecting future demand, and proposing actionable strategies for conservation and equitable 
allocation, the project will help ensure that water continues to serve as a reliable resource for 
domestic consumption, food production, and economic resilience. This study is more than a 
technical assessment—it is a forward-looking effort to safeguard the region’s water future. By 
integrating hydrological science with local realities, and by fostering collaboration across sectors, 
the project aspires to contribute meaningfully to the region’s long-term environmental 
sustainability and human development

The infrastructure emphasizes sustainability and climate change adaptation. Open spaces and landscaped areas will enhance ventilation and reduce heat absorption.
Equipment procurement will include ICT systems, technical and scientific tools for training, office equipment, and modern furniture and fixtures to support both academic and hospitality functions.
The University Hotel will stand as a model of excellence, inclusivity, and sustainability—providing world-class training for students while serving the broader community with professional hospitality services.

column4: Construction of 5-Storey Multipurpose Building- Phase 1, Talakag Campus
column6:
The idea for constructing a multipurpose facility was conceived in response to the need for more facilities on campus. With greater room for computer labs, speech labs, administrative offices, and a multi-purpose hall will meet the varied needs of the school. The establishment of the multi-purpose building will alleviate the shortage on workspaces and even address the lack of parking spaces within the campus. The development of this project has been the result of careful planning and active involvement of various university stakeholders. Both male and female participants from different beneficiary groups contributed to problem identification and project design, with the process grounded in gender analysis to address gender-specific issues. Feedback gathered during stakeholder consultations emphasized the urgent need for additional classrooms, laboratories and office spaces where growing student numbers—both male and female—are straining current facilities. Spanning a total land area of 684 square meters, the five-storey project has a proposed total investment of Php 50 million for its first phase, with completion expected in three phases. Once completed, the building will provide essential spaces, including offices, laboratories, classrooms, and lecture halls. The building design efficiently maximizes the limited campus area, addressing the need for both administrative and student services while enhancing learning facilities for all students. The proposed five-story multipurpose building is thoughtfully designed with gender inclusivity and accessibility at its core, ensuring it meets the diverse needs of the campus community. The building is fully equipped with special provisions for PWDs, elderly residents, and Gender and Development (GAD) initiatives, ensuring that all occupants have access to essential amenities. Restroom facilities are designed to promote inclusivity, with male and female restrooms strategically placed at both ends of the building, alongside additional gender-neutral and accessible restrooms for persons with disabilities (PWDs). This approach ensures that all students, staff, and visitors, regardless of gender or physical ability, have equal access to essential facilities. Further emphasizing inclusivity, the building integrates Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Change Adaptation (DRRCCA) standards, featuring sprinkler systems, emergency exits, fire alarms, and clear evacuation signage for the safety of all occupants. The architectural plan prioritizes versatile, sustainable spaces, incorporating passive cooling systems such as high ceilings and expansive windows to enhance energy efficiency and create comfortable environments. Ramps, designated PWD and senior facilities, and other accessibility features ensure barrier-free navigation throughout the building. Security is also a priority, with CCTV monitoring and emergency lighting systems in place to enhance safety. By
complying with all relevant building codes and regulations, this multipurpose building is designed to be a safe, functional, and inclusive space, fostering a welcoming environment for all campus stakeholders.

In the future, solar panels are planned to established in this facility to reduce its power consumption and provide innovative way to utilized renewable energy in the environment. With various usages, the facility required greater energy consumption.

column4: Generation of Higher Education Statistics, Mapping of Higher Education Institutions
column6:
The project serves as CHED’s primary mechanism for the annual generation, validation, integration, and dissemination of higher education statistics, covering enrollment, graduates, faculty, programs, HEI profile, and other core indicators. It also includes the geospatial mapping of HEIs, enabling CHED to identify geographic gaps, facilitate planning for underserved areas, and support national and local development initiatives.
Major components include:
1.	Data Collection and Validation
o	Annual submission and cleaning of HEI data from Forms A, A1, B, and institutional administrative systems.
o	Harmonization with PSA classifications, metadata standards, and data quality protocols.
2.	Geospatial Mapping and Registry Development
o	Acquisition, verification, and updating of HEI coordinates;
o	Integration with GIS platforms for spatial analysis and visualization;
o	Regular update of the Unique Institutional Identifier (UII) system.
3.	Statistical Production and Publications
o	Development of statistical bulletins, dashboards, and sector reports;
o	Time series analysis of national and regional higher education trends.
4.	Capacity Building and Cross-agency Integration
o	Training CHEDROs and HEIs on data submission, data validation, and GIS tools;
o	Establishing data-sharing linkages with PSA, DOST, DICT, and LGUs.
This project is a precursor initiative that lays the foundation for CHED’s broader digital transformation efforts, including the enterprise-level data architecture and the Higher Education Data Portal.

column4: VSU Baybay Sustainability Transition and Comprehensive Campus Infrastructure Rehabilitation Program (148 buildings)
column6:
Visayas State University (VSU) continues to expand its academic programs, research activities, and student population; however, many of its physical facilities have not been upgraded in decades. A significant number of campus buildings, constructed between the 1970s and 1990s, now exhibit evident deterioration due to age, heavy utilization, and environmental exposure. These conditions affect structural integrity, user safety, and the overall suitability of facilities for modern instruction and research.
This proposal seeks funding for the upgrading and enhancement of 148 buildings within the VSU Main Campus. The project encompasses the repair of dilapidated structural and architectural components, rehabilitation of worn-out finishes, and modernization of outdated building systems. Priority will be given to classroom buildings, student dormitories, administrative units, and research facilities that directly support the university’s core academic and service functions.
The initiative aims to: (1) restore and reinforce deteriorated building elements to ensure safety and compliance with current standards; (2) modernize learning and research spaces to accommodate updated technologies and pedagogical requirements; (3) improve dormitory conditions to promote student welfare; and (4) enhance campus resilience by upgrading electrical, plumbing, roofing, and ventilation systems.
Investing in this project will significantly improve the university’s operational efficiency and learning environment. Enhanced facilities will support high-quality instruction, strengthen research outputs, and improve overall campus experience for students, faculty, staff, and visitors. Through this undertaking, VSU reaffirms its commitment to maintaining safe, functional, and future-ready infrastructure that can sustain the growing needs of its academic community and uphold its standing as a leading institution in the region.

column4: Completion of the Covered Court of San Fernando Campus
column6:
The completion of a covered court construction project on the San Fernando campus of Bukidnon State University signifies the concluding phase and represents a momentous achievement for the campus. These structures offer protection from inclement weather, enabling the continuation of activities irrespective of the weather, thereby cultivating an atmosphere of consistency and fortitude on the campus and in the community that hosts them. The completion of this effort not only improves the tangible environment but also serves as an emblematic representation of advancement and dedication to the welfare and growth of the community at large. Furthermore, the completion of the covered court initiative at BukSU-San Fernando exemplifies the campus community's collective endeavors and mutual objectives. It demonstrates proficient coordination, communication, and cooperation, all of which are critical for delivering services to the entire campus community, including students, faculty, and staff. Students, faculty, and staff will benefit from a conducive environment for physical activity and recreation on the covered court, which is fundamental for their overall health and well-being. In addition to improving physical health, consistent exercise has been found to enhance cognitive function, concentration, and overall productivity. The provision of a covered court enables individuals to participate in a wide range of sports and fitness activities, despite of the weather condition, thereby promoting a campus community that values and encourages physical activity and a healthy way of life. Moreover, the establishment of a covered court at BukSU-San Fernando fosters opportunities for social engagement, collaboration, and camaraderie among the faculty, staff, and students, thereby augmenting the overall campus experience.

Sporting events and recreational activities function as mediums through which individuals can cultivate connections, encourage a feeling of inclusion and diversity, and foster a sense of belonging. Furthermore, the inclusion of a covered court will augment the allure and competitiveness of the campus, drawing in potential students, faculty, and staff, while also fortifying the campus's culture and identity as a whole. The campus atmosphere is a significant factor in influencing the whole experience of students. In addition to traditional educational environments such as classrooms, and libraries, the importance of leisure places holds considerable weight. Covered courts and embankment works are two crucial factors that make substantial contributions to the overall well-being and comprehensive growth of kids. These architectural features not only serve as venues for engaging in physical activities but also play a vital role in cultivating a feeling of community and enhancing the visual allure of the campus.

Covered courts are multifunctional architectural constructions that fulfill many roles inside an educational institution's premises. Sports facilities serve not just as areas for athletic pursuits, but also as sites for a diverse range of events, social gatherings, and recreational activities. The implementation of covered courts facilitates year-round utilization, offering protection against inclement weather conditions, a particularly crucial aspect in areas characterized by changeable climates. This practice guarantees that students are able to continuously participate in physical activities, thereby fostering a lifestyle that is both healthy and active. Within the context of campus growth, the incorporation of embankment works carries considerable significance. The implementation of elevated landscapes and green areas in these works not only enhances the visual attractiveness of the campus, but also promotes its environmental sustainability. The integration of retaining walls is a crucial factor in the achievement of successful embankment works. These structures are specifically engineered to mitigate soil erosion and maintain the stability of raised terrains.

Bukidnon State University San Fernando Campus is underpinned by a compelling rationale rooted in safety, preservation, and environmental stewardship. Firstly, the safety and security of the campus community are paramount. Given the geographical location of the campus, it may be susceptible to landslides, erosion, and geological hazards, posing significant risks to students, faculty, and staff as well as campus infrastructure. By implementing embankment and slope protection measures, the university aims to mitigate these risks and create a safer environment for all. This project is motivated by the imperative to preserve valuable campus infrastructure. BukSU San Fernando Campus likely houses critical academic buildings and dormitories. Unchecked erosion and landslides can cause substantial damage to these structures over time. By investing in embankment and slope protection, the university seeks to safeguard its physical assets, reducing the financial burden of future repairs and reconstruction. Moreover, the above-mentioned project aligns with the principles of environmental protection. The covered court is situated in an ecologically sensitive area, uncontrolled soil erosion and landslides can disrupt the local ecosystem, including nearby creeks and forests. Proper slope protection measures will help minimize soil erosion and runoff, contributing to the maintenance of the ecological balance in the community. The deliberate arrangement of retaining walls can generate organic tiers and levels, maximizing spatial utilization and offering aesthetic appeal.
Also, it includes two (2) additional bays for the covered court. Since the location of the covered court is within the inclined area, there will be a storage room below the covered court with cemented flooring. In the pursuit of offering students’ comprehensive educational experiences, the significance of the interplay between retaining walls and covered courts becomes of utmost importance for educational institutions. The use of this comprehensive
approach guarantees that the campus setting fosters physical health, interpersonal engagement, and ecological preservation, so establishing a cohesive and enhancing environment for the academic community.

column4: Construction and Operationalization of  Environmental Biogeochemistry and Pesticides Laboratory in MSU-General Santos
column6:
The proposed Environmental Biogeochemistry and Pesticides Laboratory at Mindanao State University–General Santos City (MSU-GSC) responds to the region’s growing need for advanced environmental monitoring and scientific analysis. Located in the agriculturally dynamic but environmentally vulnerable SOCCSKSARGEN region, MSU-GSC is strategically positioned to address pressing concerns arising from intensive farming, rapid industrial expansion, and climate-related impacts. The increasing use of agricultural pesticides has raised serious issues regarding water contamination, soil degradation, biodiversity loss, and food safety—yet the region currently lacks the technical capacity, facilities, and expertise to conduct comprehensive pesticide residue and biogeochemical analyses. This gap not only limits the ability of local governments and regulatory bodies to implement evidence-based environmental management but also hinders the development of sustainable agricultural practices. Additionally, researchers and students across private and public institutions face limited access to high-level analytical resources necessary for scientific inquiry and innovation.

Establishing this laboratory will empower MSU-GSC to serve as a regional hub for environmental research, advanced analytics, and capacity-building. The facility will generate high-quality scientific data that can guide policy formulation, improve environmental governance, and support climate-resilient and sustainable farming systems. Government agencies, food processing industries, and farmers' cooperatives will benefit from reliable analytical services essential for regulatory compliance and environmental risk reduction. The laboratory will also create new opportunities for graduate and undergraduate students to gain hands-on training in cutting-edge environmental science, ensuring the long-term development of local expertise in biogeochemistry, pesticide analysis, and ecosystem management. Through this initiative, MSU-GSC strengthens its role as a leader in promoting environmental protection, food safety, and sustainable development in Mindanao.

column4: Construction of the University Animal Care and Research Center (UACRC)
column6:
Mindanao State University–General Santos (MSU-GenSan) has achieved significant strides in academic quality, with many programs receiving CHED Certificates of Compliance and Level III accreditation. As part of its commitment to global competitiveness, the University aims to strengthen its research capabilities and pursue international rankings such as QS and THE. Although MSU-GenSan has established several research laboratories across various disciplines, it lacks a dedicated facility for animal-based research—an essential component for instruction, thesis work, and research in Agriculture, Fisheries, Biology, and the newly offered Doctor of Medicine program. The absence of an animal facility has also rendered the University’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) inactive, preventing compliance with national regulations such as the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485) and limiting the publication of animal-related studies in reputable scientific journals.

The proposed University Animal Care and Research Center (UACRC) seeks to address these gaps by providing a modern, fully compliant animal research facility equipped with housing for laboratory animals, quarantine rooms, storage areas, and a training space. The center will revitalize the IACUC, enabling ethical oversight of all animal experiments within and outside the University. Once operational, the UACRC will enhance instruction by serving as a venue for anatomy and physiology classes, strengthen research productivity by supporting ethically approved animal studies, and extend training on laboratory animal care to external agencies and institutions across SOCSARGEN. By enabling the publication of undergraduate, graduate, and faculty research, as well as offering services such as training, animal breeding, and consultation, the UACRC will contribute not only to instruction, research, and extension but also to income generation—solidifying its role as a vital institutional asset for MSU-GenSan and the region.

column4: Construction of Halal Training Center
column6:
The proposed Halal Learning Resource and Training (HLRT) Center is envisioned as a premier hub for halal education, capacity building, and industry development in the region. Its core function is to facilitate high-quality trainings, seminars, workshops, and forums for individuals and enterprises seeking to enter or advance in halal production, manufacturing, and processing. The Center will host a wide range of programs designed to disseminate accurate and comprehensive information on halal principles and practices, ensuring that all activities and training modules strictly adhere to internationally accepted halal certification standards. To guarantee global credibility, the facility will engage reputable resource speakers, trainers, and lecturers from countries with well-established halal industries such as the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.

Beyond training, the HLRT Center will support halal industry development through specialized programs focused on priority sectors such as tuna products, fish feeds, and cosmetics. These initiatives will produce highly skilled personnel capable of contributing to the growth of the regional halal economy. The facility will house a dedicated laboratory for training purposes and a state-of-the-art analytical services laboratory equipped with modern molecular and biochemical testing technologies essential for halal validation. At the heart of the building, a multimedia-equipped halal learning resource library will provide accessible knowledge materials for students, researchers, and industry players. Serving as a multidisciplinary convergence point, the HLRT Center will unite Islamic scholars, educators, scientists, entrepreneurs, workers, certification bodies, and government and non-government agencies. Through these linkages, the Center will play a pivotal role in strengthening the halal ecosystem and supporting the development of a vibrant, sustainable halal industry in the region.

column6:

As a green science facility, the project incorporates climate change adaptation measures, such as energy-efficient lighting, proper waste disposal systems, and provisions for renewable energy integration. column4: Solar-Powered Sustainable Water Distribution and Drainage Improvement, and Road Network Expansion — Main Campus
column6:
This project entails a comprehensive upgrade of the campus’s water resource distribution system, enhancement of its drainage infrastructure, and construction of an integrated internal road network. The interventions are strategically designed to promote efficient water supply, mitigate flooding and surface runoff, and ensure safe, accessible internal mobility.
Key features of the upgrade include the installation of a 2-kilometer underground pipe network to distribute water across the campus; the implementation of a rainwater harvesting system coupled with a 40,000-liter elevated water storage tank, positioned at the highest elevation point on campus to maximize gravity-fed supply. Complementing this, a solar-powered water pump will be installed, ensuring energy-efficient water delivery and reducing long-term operational costs. Additionally, infrastructure at lower-lying areas will be elevated to prevent waterlogging and improve drainage.
Through the upgraded water distribution and drainage systems, the project will meet the institution’s operational needs, increase resilience against climate-related events, and improve the reliability of water services campus-wide. The newly developed road network will facilitate smooth vehicular and pedestrian movement, enhance connectivity between key campus buildings, and accommodate future expansion.

column4: Establishment of Underground Water System Phase I of Phase II
column6:
Phase I of the underground water system involves the initial groundwork essential for establishing a reliable and sustainable water supply. This phase begins with a site assessment and survey, where detailed mapping and surveying of the campus are conducted to determine the most optimal location for the water system. Following this, excavation and trenching activities are carried out to establish underground pipelines for water distribution. The development of the water source includes the installation of a water well or borehole to access groundwater. Additionally, essential water pumps and filtration systems are installed to ensure a safe and consistent water supply. The phase concludes with initial testing to assess water quality and verify the proper functionality of the system.
The Construction of Underground Water System Phase I will deliver essential infrastructure components that will establish a reliable and sustainable water supply system for the institution. Under General Requirements, the project will undertake the mobilization and demobilization of resources, secure all necessary permits and clearances, implement comprehensive construction safety and health measures, and provide temporary facilities to support uninterrupted operations. Site works will include 89 square meters of clearing and grubbing within the project area, drilling works for the water source, and the preparation of 80 square meters of gravel bedding to ensure a stable foundation for structural components. The project will proceed with plain and reinforced concrete works, consisting of 15.20 cubic meters of Class A structural concrete, 456 kilograms of reinforcing steel bars, and the installation of formworks and falseworks to support concrete placement. For the pump house and filtration house, civil and finishing works will include 139.97 square meters of  masonry construction, 279.94 square meters of cement plaster finishing, painting works of equal coverage, installation of 20 lengths of HDPE pipes and fittings, 70 lengths of structural metal works, and 23 lengths of roofing materials. The project will further deliver the supply, delivery, and installation of key equipment and materials, including a 15 HP submersible pump and motor, a 54-cubic-meter elevated steel water storage tank, a 37.5 KVA three-phase transformer for the water pump, a complete filtration system, and a 10-cubic-meter steel ground tank. Lastly, comprehensive electrical works and lighting fixtures will be installed to ensure the full functionality and operational safety of the entire water system. Upon completion, Phase I will establish the foundational facilities and equipment necessary to support a dependable underground water distribution system for the campus.

column4: Establishment of Power House with Generator Set Installation
column6:
The Generator Sets and Powerhouse project aims to ensure a reliable backup power supply for the campus by installing dedicated generator sets and constructing a power facility. This facility will accommodate essential components such as the generators themselves, electrical control panels, and fuel storage tanks necessary for the smooth and safe operation of the system. Phase I of the project will cover the design and construction of the powerhouse structure, followed by the installation of generator sets that can handle the campus’s peak electricity demand. It will also include the setup of electrical control systems to manage power flow and a fuel storage system to support continuous operation during outages. The phase will conclude with thorough testing and commissioning to verify that all systems are functioning according to specifications.
The Generator Sets and Powerhouse project includes several key activities to ensure a fully functional and reliable backup power system for the campus. These activities begin with Site Preparation, which involves clearing and preparing the site for construction, including excavation and laying the foundation. This is followed by the Construction of the Powerhouse, which entails building the structural framework, such as walls, roofing, flooring, and incorporating safety measures for both equipment and personnel.
Next is the Installation of Generator Sets, where the selected generators—based on the campus’s peak power needs—are installed along with the fuel storage system and related electrical systems. The Electrical Setup includes installing control panels, power distribution boards, and automatic transfer switches to facilitate seamless switching between the main power supply and the backup generator. Finally, the project concludes with Testing and Commissioning, which ensures that all generators, control systems, and electrical setups are fully operational through load testing and operational simulation.
The Construction of the Powerhouse with Generator Set begins with the General Requirements, which include Mobilization and Demobilization activities to facilitate the movement of personnel, equipment, and materials to and from the site. It also covers securing all necessary Permits and Clearances to ensure compliance with regulations, as well as implementing Construction Safety and Health measures to maintain a safe working environment. Temporary Facilities will be provided to support construction operations, and complete As-Built Drawings will be prepared and submitted upon project completion.
For the Site Work, the project involves Excavation totaling 29 cubic meters to prepare the foundation and structural base of the powerhouse. Additionally, 2.85 cubic meters of Gravel Fill will be placed to create a stable, compacted base for the structure.
For the Plain and Reinforced Concrete Work, the scope includes 48.85 cubic meters of Concrete Works, forming the primary structural elements of the powerhouse. The installation of 2,787.93 kilograms of Reinforcing Steel Bars provides the necessary tensile strength for structural stability. Formworks and Falseworks are also required to properly shape and support the concrete during curing, ensuring precision and quality.
Under Finishing and Other Civil Works, Soil Poisoning will be applied to protect the structure from termite damage. 111.26 square meters of Masonry Works and 372.52 square meters of Plastering Works will provide durable and smooth wall surfaces, while Painting Works of the same area will enhance aesthetics and surface protection. Plumbing Works and Fixtures are included to ensure proper water supply and drainage within the facility.
For Metal Works, the project includes the installation of 421.36 linear meters of Steel Ladder to provide safe vertical access, as well as 2 sets of Roll-Up and Louvers to facilitate ventilation and equipment access. For Doors and Windows, the project covers the supply and installation of all required doors and windows to provide security, ventilation, and natural lighting. Under Electrical Works, the scope includes the installation of the Generator Set and energization to provide power for the facility. Additional Electrical Works and Lighting Fixtures will ensure adequate illumination and electrical functionality throughout the powerhouse.

and evidence-based training and development programs that
address current performance gaps, evolving competency needs,
and institutional goals.

competencies aligned with Outcomes-Based Education
(OBE), CHED Memorandum Orders (e.g., CMO No. 37, s.
2012 – Revised Policies on Outcomes-Based Education),
and evolving higher education trends including AI, digital
pedagogy, and flexible learning.

building programs under the CASTLE framework (TULAY,

and Transformational Leadership) for teaching staff and
HRMDO-specific learning paths for non-teaching personnel,
ensuring customized, need-based learning interventions.

including:

deliverables;
 Limited faculty capacity in AI, assessment, and curriculum
review;

development goals, including:
 UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4: Ensure
inclusive and equitable quality education and promote
lifelong learning opportunities for all.
 SDG 8: Promote sustained, inclusive, and sustainable
economic growth, full and productive employment, and
decent work for all.

column4: Gender and Development (GAD) Knowledge Management System
column6:
Over the past years, the division has implemented various
internally-funded transdisciplinary, interdisciplinary, and
multidisciplinary projects. In 2023, the division had nine (9)
completed projects implemented by forty-four (44) researchers,
that is eighteen (18) males and twenty-six (26) females; while
there are fifteen (15) ongoing projects implemented by sixty-nine

(69) researchers, composed of twenty-five (25) males and forty-
four (44) females, carried over from 2024, and eight (8) for 2025

implemented by fifty-eight (58) researchers, that is, eighteen (18)
males and forty (40) females (see Tables 1-3 in the attached
HGDG Reviewed-proposal).
Aside that the project teams are composed of men and women researchers from both the academic and administrative clusters,
ranging from staff to unit heads, faculty to division directors, and
even executives, students and alumni are also included in the
team, particularly as hired enumerators, field supervisors,
transcribers, and research assistants. This is to ensure that our
programs, activities, and projects compass to different expertise,
background, sexual orientations, and ages, providing equal
opportunities for all.
Despite the extensive collection of rich primary and secondary
data through field surveys, focus group discussions, and key
informant interviews, the division currently lacks an
institutionalized and integrated system to store, organize, and
manage this valuable information. Although terminal reports are
submitted promptly and are maintained by the RDID, the absence
of a centralized Knowledge Management System (KMS)
significantly hinders data accessibility, continuity, and effective
utilization—especially in informing gender and development
(GAD) planning, policy formulation, and impact assessment
among men and women researchers and policy-makers.
Establishing a GAD-focused Knowledge Management System is
therefore essential to ensure that data is systematically preserved,
readily retrievable, and strategically leveraged for evidence-based
decision-making and inclusive development outcomes.
In this context, the Research Development and Innovation Division
proposes the establishment of a Gender and Development
Knowledge Management System (GADKMS). This is a
centralized, user-friendly, and academically grounded platform
that is dedicated to organizing, archiving, sharing, and sustaining
gender-related research knowledge within the College.
Access to GAD-related research outputs, data, and resources
remains fragmented, limiting the academic community’s ability to
generate research that meaningfully addresses gender issues.
The GADKMS is designed to bridge this gap by serving as a
structured digital repository for gender-focused studies,
institutional GAD-related data, research tools, policies, and best
practices. Through this platform, all researchers, including faculty,
staff, and students across all clusters and institutes, and all gender
identities and sexual orientations, will have the capacity to produce
and access credible, up-to-date information that reflects the
complex realities of gender in various social, economic, and
cultural contexts.
More than a digital archive, the GADKMS will serve as a strategic
tool that enhances and monitors gender sensitivity across all
phases of research, which will range from design to data
collection, analysis, and dissemination. It will also foster
collaboration among scholars and contribute to developing
evidence-based policies and programs informed by inclusive, rigorous, and socially aware research.

Through this initiative, NBSC reaffirms its role as a research-
oriented institution that champions social equity, academic

excellence, and gender justice. The Gender and Development
Knowledge Management System stands as both a practical
solution and a strategic long-term investment in the creation of
knowledge that empowers and includes all members of society.

column4: GADKalinga: A Gender- Responsive Extension Program (GREP), Community-Based Approach
column6:
Indigenous people-men, women, children, and adults, often face extreme poverty, higher rates of landlessness, malnutrition, internal displacement, illiteracy, and unemployment compared to non-Indigenous populations. These disparities are rooted in historical injustices, colonization, and ongoing discrimination, making support essential to promote equity and justice. Supporting Indigenous people helps preserve their unique cultures, languages, traditions, and knowledge that have been passed down for generations. Recognizing and respecting their rights counters discrimination and invisibility, empowers communities, and fosters cultural resilience. Indigenous people manage about 20% of the world’s land and are proven biodiversity and natural resources custodians. Their traditional knowledge and sustainable food systems contribute significantly to protecting ecosystems, combating climate change, and enhancing resilience to natural disasters. For example, deforestation rates on Indigenous lands are substantially lower than global averages, and these lands harbor rich biodiversity comparable to protected reserves. Supporting Indigenous land rights and stewardship is vital for global environmental sustainability. Social media engages with Indigenous people through education, volunteering, advocacy, and amplifying their voices. It promotes broader public understanding and solidarity. It also helps dismantle harmful myths and supports policy changes that protect Indigenous rights and well-being. In summary, we help Indigenous peoples to rectify historical and ongoing injustices, preserve invaluable cultural and environmental heritage, support sustainable stewardship of the planet, and promote their economic and social empowerment for a fairer,
healthier world. The GADKalinga: A Gender and Development Community-Based Project addresses critical issues identified within the Bukidnon Tribe community, particularly the Sinontao Clan Cultural Village in Barangay Santiago. These issues have been classified into several key considerations that the project aims to resolve through a holistic, sustainable, and gender-responsive approach.

column4: Project KABILIN+: Kaabin sa Kinadaan, Kabuhat sa Kabilin (Project Heritage+: Partnerships in Tradition, Transforming Inheritance)
column6:
Project KABILIN+ is an initiative aimed at expanding Indigenous
partnerships for sustainable agriculture, forest conservation, and
community livelihood development in Bukidnon for better futures.
Building on the foundation of its predecessor, the Project MOCHA,
this project addresses the challenges of commercialization,
fragmented supply chains, limited market access, and
environmental threats that hinder the economic potential of indigenous farmers and forest-dependent communities. The lack
of integrated management strategies for indigenous products not
only constrains income generation but also exacerbates
deforestation and biodiversity loss, necessitating a holistic and
community-driven approach.
The project seeks to strengthen indigenous partnerships, establish
start-up businesses for indigenous communities, improve
production efficiency, promote forest conservation, enhance
market access, and advocate for policy support. Through training
programs, value chain development, and sustainable agroforestry

practices, the initiative aims to increase productivity, reduce post-
harvest losses, and improve the market competitiveness of these

indigenous products, therefore elevating community livelihood.
Additionally, the project will foster environmental sustainability
through climate-smart agricultural techniques and community-led
conservation efforts.
The expected impact of Project KABILIN+ includes increased
economic opportunities for indigenous farmers, improved
environmental resilience, and stronger policy frameworks
supporting sustainable agriculture and forest management. By
integrating more indigenous food products into the value chain
alongside coffee, honey, and adlay, the project will diversify
income sources, reinforce traditional ecological knowledge, and
contribute to long-term rural development in Bukidnon.

column6:

learning support system through:

3. Indigenous knowledge-infused Big Books for storytelling and cultural continuity

The project incorporates inclusive education principles, ensuring that the materials accommodate diverse learners, including IP children, struggling readers, and multi-grade classes.

column5: University of Science and Technology of Southern Philippines
column6:

This issue is particularly pronounced in Northern Mindanao, where only a handful of state universities and colleges offer a Bachelor of Science in Nursing program, despite a growing number of students aspiring to enter the field. The proposed 5-Storey College of Allied Health Sciences Academic Building at the University of Science and Technology of Southern Philippines (USTP) Cagayan de Oro campus is a timely and critical intervention designed to bridge this gap.

The new infrastructure will house a high-quality BS Nursing program, aligning with regional and national development plans to bolster the health sector. By leveraging the provisions of Republic Act 10931, the program will offer free tertiary education to underprivileged students, making a nursing career accessible to those who need it most. In exchange, the Return Service Agreement will ensure that graduates serve local communities, directly addressing the impact of migration and ensuring a sustainable health workforce. This project is a feasible and essential solution that addresses current needs and global trends, while providing tangible opportunities for Mindanaons to become future leaders in healthcare.

column4: Men’s and Women’s Dormitory
column6:
Student housing is vital for supporting academic performance, wellbeing, and overall campus life. As MSU-Gensan continues to grow in enrollment and expand its academic offerings, the demand for accessible and safe on-campus accommodation has outpaced the university’s existing facilities. Currently, the lack of a dedicated Men’s and Women’s Dormitory forces many students especially those from geographically distant and rural communities to seek off-campus boarding arrangements. These boarding houses vary significantly in safety, cost, and living conditions, placing students at risk and creating added financial and emotional burdens that can impede their academic performance. This concern has been consistently highlighted in institutional assessments, including AACCUP accreditation visits, which identify student housing as a critical gap that must be addressed to strengthen the university’s support systems and overall learning environment.
The construction of a new Men’s and Women’s Dormitory is therefore essential to enhancing MSU-Gensan’s capacity to provide student-centered services aligned with standards of quality, safety, and inclusivity. A modern, well-designed dormitory will not only offer a secure and conducive living environment but also promote academic focus, student retention, and overall wellbeing. Investing in such a facility is a proactive measure that supports the university’s long-term vision of fostering an equitable, supportive, and future-ready educational community.

The establishment of a Training and Research Center for Precision Agriculture Technology aims to address these challenges. This center will align with national and regional development plans by enhancing agricultural productivity and sustainability. It will also support current initiatives in modernizing farming practices while keeping up with global trends in smart agriculture and automation.
With globalization reshaping production processes, it is essential for local farmers and agricultural professionals to adopt advanced technologies, such as data-driven decision-making, precision irrigation, and automated farming systems. By equipping stakeholders with the right knowledge and tools, the project ensures a sustainable and competitive agricultural industry.

The Integrated Technology Building at USTP Oroquieta is envisioned as a state-of-the-art facility designed to advance the university’s commitment to technological innovation and education. This building will serve as a cornerstone for the Technology and Livelihood Education (TLE) Program, providing modern laboratory equipment, tools, and learning spaces essential for fostering hands-on, experiential learning. By supporting the internationalization of education and incorporating local-to-global perspectives, the Integrated Technology Building seeks to elevate USTP Oroquieta as a hub for technological and livelihood innovation. column4: Student Housing Capacity Expansion and Infrastructure Development Program

column4: ENGINEER 5.0 Program: Enhancing Next-Generation Infrastructure, Engineering Education, and Research for the Fifth Industrial Revolution
column6:
ENGINEER 5.0: Enhancing Next-Generation Infrastructure, Engineering Education, and Research for the Fifth Industrial Revolution is a multi-component institutional development program of Southern Leyte State University (SLSU) that aims to transform engineering education, research, innovation, and community extension services through advanced facilities, modern learning environments, technology-driven laboratories, and resilience-centered outreach programs. The program is composed of six interrelated sub-programs and projects that collectively address critical gaps in engineering instruction, applied research capability, industry alignment, technology incubation, and local development support.

1. Engineering Academic Complex

This project involves the construction of a state-of-the-art Engineering Academic Complex that will serve as the central hub for SLSU’s Industry 5.0–aligned engineering education. The complex will house modern lecture halls, flexible learning studios, micro-credentialing spaces, collaboration rooms, simulation laboratories, and technology-integrated facilities. Designed with green building principles, it will support lifelong learning, industry partnerships, and internationalization. The EAC directly contributes to PDP outcomes on improved quality of higher education, skills upgrading, innovation capacity, and resilient infrastructure development.

2. Smart Classroom and Laboratory Enhancement Project for the Computer Engineering Department

This project upgrades existing CpE classrooms and laboratories into fully equipped smart learning spaces. The enhancement includes installation of high-performance computing systems, IoT and robotics kits, embedded systems modules, industry-standard networking infrastructure, and interactive digital teaching tools. This modernization supports PDP-RM targets on digital transformation, future-ready engineering graduates, and strengthened science, technology, and innovation (STI) ecosystems.

3. Procurement of robotics equipment for macro-credentialing of engineering, technology and education students  

This component provides robotics hardware and software platforms for interdisciplinary teaching, hands-on experimentation, and macro-credentialing in automation, robotics, and intelligent systems. The equipment supports flexible learning pathways, enhances student employability, and addresses the national demand for advanced STEM competencies. The project supports PDP outcomes related to industry-relevant skills, global competitiveness of graduates, and integration of advanced technologies in education.

4. Construction of the SLSU Technology Business Incubator Building and Pasalubong Center for Local Innovation and Entrepreneurship

This project constructs a dedicated facility that will house the LIG-ON Technology Business Incubator and a Pasalubong Center. The building will feature:
•  coworking and mentorship spaces for startups
• prototyping and fabrication rooms
• business development and training areas
• a retail section for local products by MSMEs and artisans

The TBI Building addresses the current lack of permanent innovation and enterprise development infrastructure in the province. The project supports PDP objectives on MSME growth, innovation-driven entrepreneurship, and regional inclusive development by enabling technology commercialization and livelihood opportunities.

5. Establishment and Operationalization of the Advanced Energy, Waste Systems, and Risk Reduction Engineering Research Center (AEWSR2 - ERC)

This component establishes a specialized research center with laboratories for renewable energy systems, waste-to-energy processes, environmental monitoring, and disaster risk reduction engineering. Facilities will include testing laboratories, calibration and instrumentation suites, and applied research spaces. The center responds to pressing gaps in regional research infrastructure and supports PDP goals on environmental sustainability, clean and renewable energy, solid waste management, and disaster resilience, consistent with RA 9513, RA 9003, and RA 10121.

6. Southern Leyte Integrated Community Empowerment and Resilience Program (SLiCERP)

SLiCERP delivers community-based programs and capacity-building activities on food security, climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, and local governance strengthening. Activities include training workshops, livelihood enhancement, DRRM drills, technology transfer sessions, and technical assistance to LGUs. This program component operationalizes SLSU’s extension mandate and contributes to PDP-RM outcomes on community resilience, local government capability development, poverty reduction, and sustainable development.

RESPONSIVENESS TO THE PDP / RESULTS MATRIX

The ENGINEER 5.0 Program directly supports key outcomes of the PDP 2023–2028 and its Results Matrix, specifically:

•  Enhancing the Quality and Access to Education – improving engineering learning environments and strengthening micro-credentialing systems;
•  Advancing Research, Development, and Technology – increasing regional STI capability and research infrastructure;
• Expanding Digital Transformation and Innovation – modernizing laboratories and integrating Industry 5.0 tools;
• Accelerating Climate and Disaster Resilience – establishing research facilities for energy and risk reduction and delivering community resilience programs;
• Strengthening Local Governance and Community Empowerment – providing training and technical support to LGUs through SLiCERP;
• Chapter on Economic Transformation – promoting MSME innovation and startup development through the TBI Building.

Across its components, the program enhances human capital, strengthens STI ecosystems, supports innovation-led regional development, builds climate resilience, and improves the employability of graduates in line with national and regional priorities.

column4: SLSU – LEAD Program: Advancing Lifelong Learning, Innovation and Digital Excellence
column6:
The SLSU – LEAD Program is a multi-component institutional development initiative aimed at strengthening Southern Leyte State University’s capacity to deliver lifelong learning, digital innovation, advanced laboratory instruction, and student-centered community services. The program consists of four major sub-projects: (1) the Center for Lifelong Learning and Skills Innovation (CLLSI), (2) the Integrated Green and Smart Lecture and Laboratory Complex, (3) the Construction of a Forensic Laboratory, and (4) the Student Unified Center and Community Emergency Shelter Services (SUCCESS) Building. Collectively, these infrastructure investments are designed to transform SLSU into a future-ready, inclusive, and innovation-driven university aligned with national and regional development priorities.

1. Establishment of the Center for Lifelong Learning and Skills Innovation (CLLSI)

The first component, the Center for Lifelong Learning and Skills Innovation (CLLSI), involves constructing a three-storey facility that will serve as the institutional hub for flexible learning, micro-credentialing, digital media production, and Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL). The building will house the Lifelong Learning Commons, digital media studios, instructional design laboratories, RPL assessment rooms, and a Skills Innovation Hub. Beyond physical infrastructure, the project enables digital credentialing systems, curriculum co-design mechanisms, and institutional quality assurance frameworks. CLLSI responds to PDP-RM outcomes under Human Capital Development, workforce upskilling, and lifelong learning expansion, and directly supports RA 10968 (Philippine Qualifications Framework) and CHED CMO No. 1 s. 2025 on micro-credentials.

2. Integrated Green and Smart Lecture and Laboratory Complex

The second component, the Integrated Green and Smart Lecture and Laboratory Complex, will provide a four-storey building equipped with technologically advanced classrooms, laboratories, faculty rooms, storage spaces, and essential academic facilities. The building incorporates green architecture—including vegetation zones, improved thermal regulation, and solar power integration—to model climate-responsive infrastructure. This project contributes to PDP targets on sustainable and resilient education infrastructure, inclusive teaching and learning environments, and R&D support facilities.

3. Construction of Forensic Laboratory

The third component, the Forensic Laboratory, will establish a specialized facility that supports Criminology students’ instruction and training in cybercrime, digital forensics, and investigative technologies. The laboratory equips future law enforcement professionals with the technical competencies required to address emerging cybercrime threats in the Philippines. This investment supports PDP-RM indicators on justice sector modernization, security sector human resource development, and innovation in education for public safety.

4. Construction of Student Unified Center and Community Emergency Shelter Services (SUCCESS) Building

The fourth component, the Student Unified Center and Community Emergency Shelter Services (SUCCESS) Building, serves a dual purpose: as a student engagement center for faith-based gatherings, organizational activities, and communal learning, and as an emergency shelter during natural disasters. The facility provides accessible spaces for student interaction while strengthening campus and community resilience through emergency shelter provisions. This supports PDP outcomes on disaster preparedness, resilient communities, and inclusive social development.

Together, the four sub-projects of the SLSU – LEAD Program address key development gaps in digital transformation, flexible learning infrastructure, specialized training laboratories, and student welfare and safety. The program directly supports the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023–2028, particularly:

•	Subchapter 2.2: Improve Education and Lifelong Learning;
•	Chapter 8: Advance Research, Development, Technology, and Innovation;
•	Chapter 12: Expand and Upgrade Infrastructure; and
•	Chapter 15: Accelerate Climate Action and Strengthen Disaster Resilience.

It also aligns with the Eastern Visayas Regional Development Plan (RDP) and RDIP by expanding regional human capital development, building resilient and green learning spaces, and enhancing education–industry–community linkages. Through these integrated facilities, the SLSU – LEAD Program provides the necessary infrastructure for modern education delivery, innovation ecosystems, criminology instruction, and student-centered community support—advancing SLSU’s long-term vision as a digital, green, and socially responsive Future Perfect University.
